Title: AI Is Working Overtime. So Am I

URL Source: https://almund6ef.substack.com/p/ai-is-working-overtime-so-am-i

Published Time: 2026-07-20T07:24:50+00:00

Markdown Content:
Hi, I’m Ara. Welcome to AI with Ara, a growing community for curious minds, builders, and professionals who want practical AI insights without the noise.

Every issue brings the latest AI tools, trends, simple tutorials, and real workflows you can use right away. Clear, useful, and easy to follow, so you can learn faster, work smarter, and stay ahead.

**[Sign up for free](https://almund6ef.substack.com/).** Get smarter. Get confident. Grow with AI.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!J9TL!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_lossy/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dc24330-354d-4fdf-87e2-f667c3ecf098_498x373.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!J9TL!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6dc24330-354d-4fdf-87e2-f667c3ecf098_498x373.gif)

You open your laptop and there are three new AI features in apps you already knew how to use. Your inbox has a “summarize with AI” button. Your calendar wants to draft your replies. A coworker shares yet another tool you “have to try.” By mid afternoon your brain feels like it has twenty tabs open, none of them fully loaded.

That is AI fatigue, and it is no longer a vague complaint. Researchers, HR teams, and product designers are all studying it. It shows up in two places at once: at work, where people are told to adopt AI fast, and in everyday life, where AI has quietly slipped into almost every app and feed.

This issue breaks down what **AI fatigue** actually is, why it is spreading, and, most importantly, what you can do to feel less overwhelmed without unplugging entirely.

> **“A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.”**
> 
> Herbert A. Simon

That observation was made in 1971, but it fits the AI age remarkably well. AI can generate almost unlimited information. The scarce resource is our ability to judge what deserves attention.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RuNP!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F674ee9d3-4fe0-4eac-aaca-9a306fafee78_800x490.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RuNP!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F674ee9d3-4fe0-4eac-aaca-9a306fafee78_800x490.gif)

AI use at work continues to increase.

_**As of February 2026, Gallup reported that half of U.S. employees used AI in their jobs at least a few times a year. Twenty-eight percent used it a few times a week or more, and 13% used it daily.**_

However, access to AI is not the same as having a clear AI strategy. Employees may be told to “use AI more” without being told:

*   Which tasks AI should handle

*   Which tools are approved

*   What information must remain private

*   How thoroughly an output should be checked

*   Who is responsible when AI makes a mistake

*   When working without AI is the better choice

This uncertainty creates pressure.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OYpf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa716e675-0ea4-4cd7-8b0b-068cda163beb_1200x1200.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OYpf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa716e675-0ea4-4cd7-8b0b-068cda163beb_1200x1200.jpeg)

Pew Research Center found that 52% of U.S. workers felt worried about how AI may be used in the workplace in the future. Thirty-three percent felt overwhelmed, while 36% felt hopeful.

These numbers show that people are not simply excited or opposed to AI. Many are trying to understand where it fits while the technology, workplace expectations, and risks continue to change.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2eP8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faca06286-2966-4568-ba84-1915959bae46_1491x1055.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!2eP8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faca06286-2966-4568-ba84-1915959bae46_1491x1055.png)

AI fatigue is not one thing. It is a stack of smaller strains that pile up:

*   **Tool overload.** Too many platforms, dashboards, and features to keep track of.

*   **Verification burden.** The tiring work of checking whether the AI output is right.

*   **Prompt exhaustion.** The effort of rephrasing again and again to get a usable answer.

*   **Keeping-up anxiety.** The nagging sense that everyone else has figured out a tool you have not.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jyo-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F06f8078c-e65b-4a06-8310-25a8019a46fa_1125x726.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!jyo-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F06f8078c-e65b-4a06-8310-25a8019a46fa_1125x726.png)

A 2026 review of 22 studies found that AI can reduce administrative work in some settings. However, poorly designed systems can also create new monitoring tasks, confusion, stress, and reduced professional control. The authors concluded that AI fatigue should not be treated only as an individual self-care problem. Employers and technology designers also influence it.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K49-!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F443ee4f1-f229-4599-b6e1-db75c8c270cc_888x449.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!K49-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F443ee4f1-f229-4599-b6e1-db75c8c270cc_888x449.png)

A worker may use one tool for writing, one for meetings, one for presentations, one for research, and another for images. Each tool has its own account, settings, interface, update schedule, subscription, and privacy rules. Instead of asking, “How do I finish this task?” the person begins asking:

*   Which AI should I use?

*   Which version is best?

*   Is this tool approved?

*   Can I share this information?

*   Should I use a different model?

*   Do I need a better prompt?

The tools meant to simplify work have created a new layer of decisions.

Suppose a marketer asks AI for 25 campaign headlines.

The tool completes the request in seconds. The marketer must now read all 25, remove repeated ideas, identify brand risks, check whether claims are accurate, and choose one.

AI saved writing time but created 25 small decisions.

This pattern is common:

**Generate → compare → revise → generate again → compare again**

The person finishes with more content, but not always with more clarity.

Upwork surveyed 2,500 executives, full-time employees, and freelancers. While 96% of executives expected AI to improve productivity, 77% of employees using AI said it had increased their workload.

Why?

*   **39% spent more time reviewing or moderating AI content**

*   **23% spent more time learning the tools**

*   **21% were asked to complete more work because of AI**

This is the difference between **generation time** and **completion time**.

A report may take one minute to generate. It is not complete until someone has checked the research, removed unsupported claims, improved the logic, and made it useful.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ArDi!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff2876359-b715-4388-bd3f-e3a41171f94a_810x520.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ArDi!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff2876359-b715-4388-bd3f-e3a41171f94a_810x520.png)

Most employees did not have unlimited concentration before AI arrived.

Microsoft’s workplace telemetry found that highly active users could be interrupted by meetings, emails, or chats every two minutes during core working hours. The same research found that 60% of meetings were unscheduled or held on short notice.

Adding AI to this environment can create another stream of output to review.

The worker is no longer only answering emails and attending meetings. They may also be checking summaries, reviewing AI-generated replies, comparing automated recommendations, and watching agent activity.

AI may accelerate individual steps while making the overall workday more fragmented.

AI does not have one universal effect on productivity. The result depends on:

*   The type of task

*   The worker’s experience

*   The amount of context required

*   The quality of the AI system

*   The cost of checking mistakes

*   How well the tool fits the workflow

A study of 5,179 customer support agents found that generative AI increased issues resolved per hour by 14% on average. Newer and less-skilled workers improved the most, by 34%, while experienced workers saw smaller gains.

The tool worked because it supported a clear task within an existing customer service process.

A 2025 randomized study tested experienced open-source developers working on familiar codebases. They expected AI to make them 24% faster, but the results showed they took 19% longer.

Reviewing suggestions, fixing unsuitable code, waiting for responses, and explaining project context added extra time. The findings were based on early-2025 tools and may not apply to every developer or coding task.

The lesson is simple:

> **Fast output does not always mean faster completion.**

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nHNF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faddcb482-efb4-415f-8106-53381b1aeb3f_1281x662.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!nHNF!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faddcb482-efb4-415f-8106-53381b1aeb3f_1281x662.png)

A manager asks an employee to review customer complaints and suggest three improvements. The employee uses AI and submits a polished 10-page report. But the report:

*   Misses the main customer complaint

*   Does not explain the cause

*   Gives no clear next step

The employee saves time, but the manager must now:

*   Review the full report

*   Check the claims

*   Add the missing context

*   Complete the analysis

BetterUp and Stanford’s Social Media Lab call this **workslop**.

In a 2025 survey:

*   **40%** of U.S. desk workers said they received workslop in the previous month

*   Each case took nearly **two hours** to fix

**AI does not improve productivity when it only shifts the thinking to someone else.**

AI fatigue does not mean AI is useless. Employees can experience real benefits while also feeling pressure from the technology. A May 2026 Software Finder survey of 1,013 employees who use AI at work found that:

*   62% said AI saves them time

*   58% said it makes their jobs easier

*   50% said it improves productivity

*   Employees saved an average of 5.1 hours per week

However, employees also spent an average of 3.3 hours per week learning or troubleshooting AI tools.

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gx6D!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6e9f4149-17dd-468d-b632-bd5dec9164fc_740x523.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gx6D!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6e9f4149-17dd-468d-b632-bd5dec9164fc_740x523.png)

The same survey found that:

*   16% experienced AI fatigue

*   23% reported AI-related anxiety

*   36% felt pressured to use AI without fully understanding it

*   34% received AI-related duties outside their original job description

*   36% worried that AI could replace their jobs

Gen Z employees reported the highest AI fatigue rate at 22%. Healthcare and e-commerce workers reported an even higher rate of 23%.

[![Image 10](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gn5B!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3409b63d-5adf-4f53-b6f1-dc4144bfdbaa_661x798.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Gn5B!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3409b63d-5adf-4f53-b6f1-dc4144bfdbaa_661x798.png)

[Share](https://almund6ef.substack.com/p/ai-is-working-overtime-so-am-i?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

AI can improve productivity while increasing mental pressure. Employees may save time drafting reports but still feel stressed about checking outputs, learning new tools, protecting private data, and proving their skills remain valuable.

Trust is another concern. About 51% worried about AI-powered workplace surveillance, while 58% did not trust AI to make unbiased decisions.

Successful AI adoption therefore requires more than access to tools. Companies need clear training, privacy rules, human review, and time for employees to adjust.

**Research note:** These findings come from a self-reported survey of 1,013 employees who use AI at work. They reflect employee experiences, not independently measured productivity.

[![Image 11](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7DfZ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F64dd789d-4f45-4bc1-936a-02b476f1c431_879x561.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!7DfZ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F64dd789d-4f45-4bc1-936a-02b476f1c431_879x561.png)

Consumers may experience AI fatigue even when they do not deliberately open an AI chatbot.

AI now appears in:

*   Search summaries

*   Shopping recommendations

*   Customer support

*   Photo editing

*   Streaming suggestions

*   Social media feeds

*   Navigation

*   Personal finance tools

*   Health information

The common issue is not always the presence of AI. It is the feeling of having little control over when it appears.

_**Pew Research found that 59% of U.S. adults felt they had little or no control over how AI was used in their lives. Fifty-five percent wanted more control.**_

A customer trying to fix a billing error gets stuck in a chatbot loop. None of the options fit, the answers stay generic, and the issue must be explained again to a human agent.

AI should shorten the path to a solution, not add more steps.

You may need to change your AI habits when:

*   You open several tools before starting one task

*   You generate more versions than you use

*   You keep prompting after receiving a usable answer

*   You spend longer checking the output than creating it

*   You feel unable to begin without AI

*   You finish with information but no clear decision

*   You regularly correct vague AI work from coworkers

*   You feel pressure to test every new tool

*   You produce more but complete less

The strongest warning sign is this:

**AI is creating more decisions than it is removing.**

[![Image 12](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LdMb!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a004741-6d1f-4a9c-84d6-821d50981f81_1062x589.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!LdMb!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1a004741-6d1f-4a9c-84d6-821d50981f81_1062x589.png)

AI is usually more useful when the task is:

*   **Clear:** You can describe the expected result.

*   **Repeatable:** You complete the same type of work regularly.

*   **Reviewable:** You can check whether the answer is correct.

*   **Low risk:** A mistake can be identified and fixed.

*   **Time consuming but simple:** The task requires effort more than deep judgment.

Examples include organizing meeting notes, creating an initial outline, categorizing feedback, reformatting information, or generating a small number of alternatives.

Consider skipping AI when:

*   You already know exactly what you want to say

*   The task requires personal experience

*   Someone needs empathy rather than speed

*   The information is private or confidential

*   You cannot properly verify the answer

*   The decision affects health, employment, safety, finances, or legal rights

*   The tool is turning a simple task into a complicated process

Not every blank page is a productivity problem.

Sometimes thinking without assistance is part of understanding the problem.

[![Image 13](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-GRK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c525e27-2e3a-4fa4-8c1a-b5a905c6861a_1121x583.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!-GRK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F1c525e27-2e3a-4fa4-8c1a-b5a905c6861a_1121x583.png)

Before using AI, ask four questions.

AI is useful for repeated tasks such as formatting notes, creating basic summaries, categorizing information, or preparing a first outline.

You should have enough knowledge, evidence, or trusted sources to check the result. Do not rely heavily on AI when you cannot tell whether the answer is correct.

A weak headline can be changed. A private data leak, harmful medical recommendation, legal mistake, or unfair employment decision may be much harder to correct. The higher the consequence, the more human control is required.

Consider privacy, consent, accuracy, fairness, confidentiality, and the people affected by the result. If a task fails the responsibility test, do not put it into an AI tool. AI is usually a stronger fit when the task is repeatable, reviewable, reversible, and responsible.

Avoid AI when:

*   You already know what you want to say

*   The task needs personal experience or honest opinion

*   Someone needs empathy, not speed

*   The information is confidential

*   The decision affects health, employment, money, safety, or legal rights

*   You cannot verify the answer

*   The tool makes a simple task harder

*   You are using it only because others are

Thank-you notes, apologies, sensitive feedback, hiring decisions, and responses to worried employees often need human judgment.

Not every moment needs to be optimized.

[![Image 14](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NwVV!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F445c0d1b-aa0b-4009-8056-1e3667f3cf87_732x757.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!NwVV!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F445c0d1b-aa0b-4009-8056-1e3667f3cf87_732x757.png)

*   **3 prompt rounds**

Limit each task to three useful prompts. Then choose the best result, edit it yourself, or restart with a clearer plan.

*   **2 trusted sources**

Check important claims against at least two credible sources, especially for health, finance, laws, statistics, or product claims. AI output is not a source.

*   **1 AI-free focus block**

Set aside 30 to 45 minutes each day without chatbots, notifications, or automated suggestions. Use the time to think, read, plan, write, or solve problems independently.

You do not need to stop using AI. You need clearer limits.

Choose one main AI tool for daily work. Keep another only if it serves a different purpose.

**Action:** Remove tools that do the same job.

Know what you need before opening AI.

Instead of:

“Help me with this project.”

Try:

“Create a five-point newsletter outline.”

**Action:** Finish this sentence first:

“I am using AI to create ______.”

More output creates more decisions. Ask for:

*   Three headlines, not 20

*   Five ideas, not 30

*   Two versions, not 10

**Action:** Limit most requests to three to five options.

Use one prompt to create, one to correct, and one to improve.

After that, choose the best result and finish it yourself.

**Action:** Do not keep generating versions without a clear reason.

Do not write, check, edit, and regenerate at the same time. First, create the draft. Then review:

*   Facts

*   Sources

*   Tone

*   Privacy

*   Missing context

**Action:** Separate AI generation from human review.

Do not count only the time AI takes to generate an answer. Include:

*   Prompting

*   Reading

*   Fact-checking

*   Rewriting

*   Formatting

A one-minute draft may still become a 20-minute task.

**Action:** Compare the full completion time with doing the task yourself.

Use AI when it removes work. Stop using it when it creates more checking, more choices, or more confusion.

*   AI can save time, improve access to information, support less experienced workers, and remove repetitive work.

*   It can also create endless options, shallow output, verification pressure, and another reason to stay connected.

*   The difference is not simply whether someone uses AI.

*   It is whether the use has a clear purpose, a finish line, and a human decision-maker.

Before opening an AI tool, ask one question:

**Will this make the task lighter, or will it give me one more thing to manage?**

Use AI when it reduces effort. Close it when it starts competing for your attention.

[Share](https://almund6ef.substack.com/p/ai-is-working-overtime-so-am-i?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

Phew! That was a lot, right? But hey, knowledge is power🌟. We hope this edition gave you some insights and maybe even cleared up a few doubts.

Title: The biggest technical SEO time-wasters to avoid

URL Source: https://searchengineland.com/technical-seo-waste-time-482608

Published Time: 2026-07-20T12:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
[Technical SEO](https://searchengineland.com/guide/what-is-technical-seo) is full of recommendations, but not all of them deserve the same priority. A task that’s critical for one website may not be worth the effort on another.

Instead of chasing green audit scores or clearing every warning in your [SEO](https://searchengineland.com/guide/what-is-seo) tool, focus on the activities that will have the greatest impact. The best technical SEOs prioritize what’s needed over what’s most obvious.

## Why prioritizing technical SEO is important

When you’re considering a technical SEO task, it’s important to prioritize it against the other work competing for your time.

### You have limited time

You have limited time and resources. It isn’t possible to tackle every task on your to-do list, so you need to identify which activities deserve the highest priority.

Focus on the activities that will deliver the biggest results for the time you invest.

### You have limited developer resources

Technical SEO tasks often require help from your development team. That means you’ll need to secure time in their sprint to implement them. Anyone who’s worked in SEO for any length of time knows how valuable that resource is.

Make sure every request is worth your developers’ time and the tradeoff of other work they won’t be able to complete.

### You need to show impact

Every technical SEO task you take on should have a clear expected ROI. That isn’t always easy to quantify, but you should be able to explain why you’re doing it and how you expect it to move the needle.

Once you can answer those questions, you can start prioritizing technical SEO tasks against one another.

**_Dig deeper: [Where to focus technical SEO when you can’t do it all](https://searchengineland.com/technical-seo-focus-471824)_**

[Be the brand customers find first. Track, grow, and measure your visibility across Google, AI search, social, local, and every channel that influences buying decisions. Start your free trial](https://www.semrush.com/?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0101default&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## How to tell if you might be wasting time

Rather than labeling specific tasks as time-wasters, consider how to determine whether a task is worth your time on your website.

### If you’re doing it to check a box

If your only reason for carrying out a technical SEO activity is to clear alerts in your SEO tool or because you saw it recommended on LinkedIn, stop. Very few, if any, technical SEO activities should be a top priority for every website.

If you don’t have a reason for doing it beyond “SEO best practice,” I’d argue it isn’t something you should dive into. Focus instead on activities that will improve your website’s performance for users and search bots.

### You can’t quantify the impact

This is perhaps the most important reason to park a technical SEO task: You don’t know what impact it will have.

If you want people to buy into your SEO plans, you need to show why they’re financially worthwhile.

That might mean improving revenue, reducing churn, or increasing qualified traffic.

For example, if you’re considering improving a page’s load speed, don’t make “reduce page load time” the goal. Instead, consider what faster load times could achieve for your organic performance and business goals.

If you work on an ecommerce site, you may know that faster load times can improve conversion rates. That’s a much stronger reason to take on the work than simply achieving a “good” page speed score.

By making conversion rate improvement the goal, you can estimate the potential financial impact. For example, if a page converts at an average rate of X% and generates $X in annual revenue, increasing the conversion rate to X+1% could generate up to $Y in additional revenue.

### You don’t know how to measure success

If you aren’t sure how you’ll measure the impact of an activity, that may be a sign it shouldn’t be a priority.

## Examples of work that can be a waste of time

Any technical SEO activity can be a time-waster. Technical SEO is about optimizing your website to provide the best possible experience for users and search bots. That means what is a waste of time for one website may be a necessary activity for another.

That said, there are several technical SEO activities I’ve seen appear on countless checklists despite offering little discernible benefit. That doesn’t mean you should remove them from your to-do list. It means they should only be there if they’ll solve a problem your website actually has.

### Core Web Vitals work when they aren’t that bad

Yes, I know Core Web Vitals scores are important. I just don’t think they’re so important that you should continually optimize them. As long as your CWVs are in the “good” range, pushing them further into that range is likely to deliver diminishing returns.

I doubt spending developer time to shave a few milliseconds off your Largest Contentful Paint score will have much impact on rankings or user behavior.

Reserve Core Web Vitals optimization for pages that genuinely aren’t meeting targets. These are the pages users struggle to load or that negatively affect usability.

Get your scores into the “good” range before investing time chasing incremental improvements.

### Removing redirects when you don’t have chains

I understand the perfectionist approach to redirects. No one likes running a crawl and seeing 301 status codes reported. However, the real concern with redirects is how they affect search bots’ ability to crawl your website.

If you aren’t seeing redirect loops, chains with more than five hops, redirects to irrelevant pages, or enough redirects to affect bots’ ability to crawl most of your website, you can probably leave them alone.

Sure, if you have a few spare minutes and you’re already in your CMS, you can update links so they point directly to the final destination instead of a redirecting URL. Realistically, though, there are only a few situations where this belongs near the top of your to-do list.

Leave redirect cleanup until it has a measurable impact on your site’s performance.

Get the newsletter search marketers rely on.

* * *

### Optimizing bot crawling when your content is already crawlable

There’s a lot of misinformation about crawl budget. For most websites, it isn’t an issue. Large enterprise websites often need to optimize crawl paths, but smaller websites usually don’t.

If your website has developed spider traps or is allowing bots to crawl pages you don’t want indexed, that’s worth addressing. Otherwise, if [Google Search Console](https://searchengineland.com/google-search-console-seo-guide-443942) shows Google is crawling your important pages, you can probably move crawl budget optimization lower on your priority list.

### Fixing every 404 status

Like fixing every 301 [redirect](https://searchengineland.com/redirects-seo-guide-442811), eliminating every link to a 404 page is often more about tidying up than solving a meaningful problem.

404s are a normal and expected part of a website. If they’re hurting the user experience, absolutely fix them. If you’re simply trying to clear the list of 404s in your crawling tool, it can probably wait until you have time.

### Removing obsolete metadata like ‘meta keywords’

I know no one is adding meta keywords anymore. That’s good. It also doesn’t mean you need to spend precious time removing them. Just leave them.

Chances are they’re so old they aren’t even giving your competitors useful hints about the keywords you’re targeting. We’ve all moved on from meta keywords, so you can, too.

### Routine disavow file maintenance

Many SEOs will tell you they don’t use disavow files at all. I agree their usefulness has diminished significantly. There may be times when you want to submit or update one.

You may also want to audit it to make sure nothing inappropriate was submitted in the past. However, I struggle to think of a reason why routinely updating a disavow file on a scheduled basis would be productive.

### Clearing audit tool issues

Not every issue your SEO tool flags is an emergency. Remember that SEO tools lack the context of your broader strategy and your website’s foundation.

You may have intentionally blocked pages in your robots.txt file or returned 404 status codes for some pages. That doesn’t mean they’re problems or that you need to fix them.

Your auditing tools should support your technical SEO work, not dictate it. You don’t need to clear every issue they report to have a technically healthy website. Don’t let the red lights and warnings distract you from more meaningful technical SEO work.

**_Dig deeper: [How to make your SEO strategy more commercially aware](https://searchengineland.com/make-seo-strategy-more-commercially-aware-481779)_**

## What to do instead

Instead of working through a technical SEO checklist, spend that time on projects that will have a greater impact.

How do you know which tasks are worth doing? Any technical SEO work should meet at least one of these three criteria.

### It directly impacts revenue or business goals

It’s much easier to get buy-in and recognition for your technical SEO work when you can tie it directly to revenue or business goals.

That means drawing a clear line between the work you’re doing and a business outcome. For example, if you’re improving slow-loading pages, you can connect that work to higher conversion rates. That’s a much stronger indicator of business value than simply making a page load faster.

### It creates a foundation for work that supports business goals

Technical SEO is worth the investment when it enables other work that will move the needle.

For example, it may be difficult to show how optimizing crawl paths on an enterprise website directly affects business goals. However, you can connect improved crawl paths to revenue-driving pages being discovered and crawled, ensuring SEO tests on those pages are found and processed.

Without crawl optimization, search bots may never see those SEO tests, making the work ineffective. Activities that enable other important SEO initiatives are valuable in their own right.

### It prepares your website for AI-driven search

A final criterion for meaningful technical SEO work is whether it prepares your website for future changes. Some work may not deliver immediate returns but could pay off over time. Preparing your website for AI-powered search experiences is one example.

You may not be getting much traffic or many conversions from AI agents yet, but there’s a strong possibility that this is where the web is heading. Preparing for that shift can feel risky because it’s speculative. However, when done well, this work is also likely to improve your website for today’s search bots and users.

[Own the conversation before your competitors. See where your brand appears, where it doesn’t, and exactly how to win more visibility across search, AI, local, social, and every channel that matters. Start your free trial](https://www.semrush.com/?utm_campaign=ic_sel_0102default&utm_source=searchengineland.com&utm_medium=overlay&onboarding=off)
## Avoid busywork, prioritize impact

Technical SEO work can be time-consuming, involve multiple teams and stakeholders, and ultimately make the difference between a well-performing website and a poor one.

The key is making sure your time and energy are spent on activities that produce meaningful results. Treat technical SEO like any other business investment: prioritize the work that’s most likely to produce meaningful results.

**_Dig deeper: [Why proving technical SEO ROI is so difficult](https://searchengineland.com/proving-technical-seo-roi-481234)_**

Title: My goal is to never apply for a marketing job ever again

URL Source: https://mariiakislykh.substack.com/p/my-goal-is-to-never-apply-for-a-marketing

Published Time: 2026-07-19T08:32:12+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1: red and white road sign](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1607877642406-7f8699aa83ca?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&fit=max&fm=jpg&ixid=M3wzMDAzMzh8MHwxfHNlYXJjaHwxfHxtb25hJTIwbGlzYSUyMHN0cmVldHxlbnwwfHx8fDE3ODQzOTU4MDN8MA&ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=80&w=1080)](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1607877642406-7f8699aa83ca?crop=entropy&cs=tinysrgb&fit=max&fm=jpg&ixid=M3wzMDAzMzh8MHwxfHNlYXJjaHwxfHxtb25hJTIwbGlzYSUyMHN0cmVldHxlbnwwfHx8fDE3ODQzOTU4MDN8MA&ixlib=rb-4.1.0&q=80&w=1080)

On how to build a brand before you need it. 

Over the last 10 years, I’ve probably had more than 50 interviews for B2B marketing roles.

Earlier in my career, I liked interviewing. It was a great way to see what the market was paying.

Then there was a time in my life when I didn’t have the luxury of being picky. I just needed a job to secure my visa so I wouldn’t get deported. It was stressful AF. I was desperately knocking on every door.

After going through so many recruitment processes, both by choice and out of necessity, I came to one conclusion:

**It’s a waste of time.**

At least the traditional process is.

You send your CV and a cover letter without really knowing who you’re applying to. The company has no idea who you are either. Then you sit around waiting for someone to call you back.

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qvI8!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fad53a71c-a21c-4e03-afc4-fc69c6a95d22_1084x326.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!qvI8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fad53a71c-a21c-4e03-afc4-fc69c6a95d22_1084x326.png)

I’d say it’s a pretty typical situation for the open marketing role

If your CV makes it through the pile of 100 applications, get ready for a marathon of interviews where you answer the same questions over and over, plus a few that make absolutely no sense.

One interviewer asked me whether I preferred cats or dogs. TRUE STORY.

Saw this the other day and it made me smile:

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xfpK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7e9b1b02-aaa1-412e-8bd7-1fc7523a1a14_1104x534.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xfpK!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7e9b1b02-aaa1-412e-8bd7-1fc7523a1a14_1104x534.png)

And let’s not forget the take home assignments.

You spend days working on them, only to hear that someone else was a better fit. Or you get an offer SO LOW that you start wondering why you bothered in the first place.

**This traditional process isn’t ideal for hiring managers either.**

Hiring someone after just a couple of hours of interviews is a gamble.

A year ago, I had an opening on my content team. It was a key role. This person would work with enterprise customers, and I needed someone who could take ownership, work independently, and be reliable.

I needed a superstar.

So I decided **not to open****the hiring process** at all.

Instead, I gave the role to someone I’d worked with before.

Everyone in the company agrees she was a superstar hire. And honestly, I don’t think we would have found someone that good through the traditional process of collecting CVs.

More and more companies don’t want to make the expensive mistake of hiring the wrong person. Instead, they turn to their networks for referrals.

It’s true for marketing roles (and really, for any job): **your CV doesn’t matter nearly as much as your reputation.**

I don’t dream of a future where I have to tailor my CV 50 different times and go through Dante’s nine circles of hell over and over again. **My goal is never to chase jobs, but to build a reputation that attracts opportunities.**

Someone once said: build your personal brand before you need it.

Since I started investing in my online presence and taking my reputation seriously, opportunities have started coming to me:

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oXuM!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5fcaab8-81dd-425f-8a3a-d8b2cbe178ef_1280x720.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oXuM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc5fcaab8-81dd-425f-8a3a-d8b2cbe178ef_1280x720.png)

Full disclosure: I’m happy in my current job. That's exactly why I think **now is the best time to future-proof my marketing career,** so that 30 years from now I won't have to explain to a robot what motivated me to apply.

I’m constantly meeting new people. And every conversation eventually gets to the same question: “So, what do you do?”

For years, my answer was always the same.

“I work in marketing.”

That was the mistake.

It was technically true, but it didn’t tell anyone anything. I never explained what kind of marketing I did, who I helped, or what problems I solved.

**Once I started being specific, people suddenly knew when to think of me.**

I’d hear things like, “Oh, you should talk to my sister. She’s looking for someone exactly like you.”

It turns out people can’t recommend you if they don’t know what to recommend you for. You don’t have to knock on every door yourself. You just have to make it easy for other people to open one for you.

**You can call me a crazy optimist, but it works.**

By the way, one of my favorite books on creating your own luck (it’s not woo woo, I promise) is _What I Wish I Knew About Luck_ by Stanford professor Tina Seelig.

This year alone, I’ve received at least six LinkedIn messages from recruiters and founders asking if I’d be interested in chatting about an open role.

During one of those virtual coffees, I asked a founder why they even bothered headhunting people.

What he said was SO BRUTAL:

_“I don’t want people who are looking for a job. If they’re unemployed, something might be wrong. I want the person everyone else wants to work with.”_

OUCH.

My face probably looked like I’d just bitten into a lemon. All I could think about was how desperate I’d once been, applying for every marketing job I could find. And there was nothing wrong with me.

But I can confirm that headhunting is still a thing.

If you want more companies to discover you, **make sure your LinkedIn profile includes the keywords for THE JOB YOU WANT**, not just the jobs you’ve had.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QqKy!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F69e2cfe6-8c0e-4728-a706-c114a240c220_1574x926.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QqKy!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F69e2cfe6-8c0e-4728-a706-c114a240c220_1574x926.png)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!st3h!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b1ec9fe-0f71-486e-8936-ca8729a4afa2_1580x696.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!st3h!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8b1ec9fe-0f71-486e-8936-ca8729a4afa2_1580x696.png)

Candidates often tailor the titles and responsibilities on their CVs to match the job ad. You can do the same with your LinkedIn profile.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!F1t4!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa498e6ea-0a2f-40ce-8a81-f5425039134d_1574x1052.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!F1t4!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa498e6ea-0a2f-40ce-8a81-f5425039134d_1574x1052.png)

Titles matter. If you can get a better title, go for it.

Add the keywords that describe the role you’d like to get throughout your profile: in your headline, your skills, your job descriptions, and even the titles of your previous roles, where appropriate.

**Titles matter for LinkedIn’s algorithm**. If a recruiter is searching for a Head of Content, but your profile only says Intern, Content Writer, and Project Manager, there’s a good chance your profile won’t show up in their search.

If you want someone to hire you to do their marketing, start by marketing yourself.

For that reason, I’d suggest picking one platform and sticking with it. LinkedIn, Substack, Medium, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, or Twitter (I refuse to call it X, Elon!!).

There’s a simple reason why.

It’s been proven that the more often we see or hear about someone, the more positively we tend to perceive them. We trust what’s familiar.

So**become familiar** by being visible on one platform.

I know it’s hard on the ego when your posts get zero likes (to be fair, I have no idea if anyone will even make it this far into my article, and that’s OK).

But you’re doing this for yourself anyway.

Just keep showing up.

As Head of Content, I mostly write about content marketing.

I share my opinions, observations, experiments, the research I’m reading, and the tactics that have worked for me.

It pushes me to get better at my job because I know I’ll eventually share those lessons with my LinkedIn people!

One person who had **never engaged with any of my posts** sent me this message:

[![Image 8](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Mb5v!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe8c550c4-a72c-4b92-8a47-82f4ce57e5e8_898x380.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Mb5v!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe8c550c4-a72c-4b92-8a47-82f4ce57e5e8_898x380.png)

I’ve lost count of how many people have told me in person that they love my content, even though they’ve never liked or commented on a single post.

On a separate note: Everyone can generate content with AI.

That’s EXACTLY why you should start writing.

People can spot AI from a mile away. What they’re craving is creativity, humor, original opinions, and insights you can only get from someone who has actually done the work.

Not another “I replaced my team with AI agents” crap.

I honestly don’t understand why people are so afraid to share their ideas.

Even during interview assignments, I always gave away my best thinking.

Why?

Because ideas are easy.

Execution is the hard part.

Whenever you meet someone, try to leave them with one **useful idea**they can actually use. Don’t gatekeep, whether you’re in an interview, networking, or replying to someone who messaged you on LinkedIn asking how you did something.

Be generous, and generosity has a way of coming back.

A recent example.

I wrote a book for content marketers on how to get promoted. Before publishing it, I wanted to see whether it actually resonated with people, so I **sent free copies to a handful of my LinkedIn connections**.

The response blew me away.

I received incredible feedback, made a few friends who are now supporting my self-publishing journey, and got confirmation that the book is genuinely useful for content marketers who want to grow into senior roles.

Btw, if that sounds like you, here’s the waiting list (I’m putting the final touches on the book!!):

[Join the waiting list](https://maya-pasek.kit.com/99db0f3a8a)

You don’t have to love your company to be professional. Do good work. Be reliable. **Leave people thinking, “I’d work with them again.”**

That’s how opportunities show up YEARS LATER.

I got my current job thanks to people I’d worked with before. We loved working together, and when an opening came up, they recommended me for the role. I’m incredibly grateful they did.

My advice is simple: don’t be a dick to the people you work with.

We all move through our careers, and you never know when your paths will cross again.

There was a time when I worried about my future career because of all the predictions that AI would cause an economic crisis, there would be fewer jobs, and blah, blah, blah.

**I stopped being anxious when I started learning**as much as my free time allowed.

I take courses, read marketing books, watch tutorials, build with AI. I follow other professionals and learn from them.

People I follow and learn from, in no particular order (and I’m sure I’ve forgotten someone!): [Kevin Indig](https://open.substack.com/users/556308-kevin-indig?utm_source=mentions), [Tayla Burrell](https://open.substack.com/users/369842061-tayla-burrell?utm_source=mentions), [George Mack](https://open.substack.com/users/18837513-george-mack?utm_source=mentions) , [Lenny Rachitsky](https://open.substack.com/users/1849774-lenny-rachitsky?utm_source=mentions) , [Ruben Hassid](https://open.substack.com/users/339636559-ruben-hassid?utm_source=mentions), [Elena Verna](https://open.substack.com/users/3478323-elena-verna?utm_source=mentions), [Lily Ray](https://open.substack.com/users/2021472-lily-ray?utm_source=mentions), [Hanna Huffman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/hannahuffman/), [Gaetano DiNardi](https://open.substack.com/users/89326649-gaetano-dinardi?utm_source=mentions), [Ina Toncheva](https://open.substack.com/users/309852232-ina-toncheva?utm_source=mentions), [Emily Kramer](https://open.substack.com/users/18675193-emily-kramer?utm_source=mentions), [Oussama Bettaieb](https://www.linkedin.com/in/oussamabettaieb/), [Irina Maltseva](https://www.linkedin.com/in/irinamaltseva/), [Dawn Halpin](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dawnhalpin/), [Matt Kenyon](https://www.linkedin.com/in/matt-kenyon-50959964/), [Josh Blyskal](https://www.linkedin.com/in/joshua-blyskal/), [Romana Kuts](https://www.linkedin.com/in/romana-kuts/), [Ryan Law](https://www.linkedin.com/in/thinkingslow/), [Cyrus Shepard](https://open.substack.com/users/3481734-cyrus-shepard?utm_source=mentions), [Olga Andrienko](https://www.linkedin.com/in/olgandrienko/).

P.S. What does it even mean to “build a career”?

For a long time, I thought it was about getting a better title or a bigger salary.

Now I think it’s about putting in the work so opportunities come to you instead of you chasing them.

As the job market becomes more unpredictable and marketing roles get harder to land, your best investment is yourself: **your visibility, your skills, and your relationships**.

That’s it.

**If you’ve made it this far, we should definitely stay in touch.**

My Substack:

[My LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/maya-kislykh/)

[My YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@mayapasek)(coming soon... subscribe if you enjoy encouraging people to make questionable life decisions)

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dLZ3!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80b525f6-c325-4106-a98f-d837272a1840_1600x900.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dLZ3!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F80b525f6-c325-4106-a98f-d837272a1840_1600x900.gif)

I ran a little research and found the actual commit messages on GitHub:

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZeJT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fba625b51-40af-41bb-ab33-d75aadfe2f74_2560x1520.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!ZeJT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fba625b51-40af-41bb-ab33-d75aadfe2f74_2560x1520.png)

My favorite: [“Change Loading to Thinking so I can join the AI bubble”](https://github.com/DJSaunders1997/GPTeasers/commit/934ac70e2733e314390939e2ba83df73e32ac82d) 😅

And this is not a niche joke: Before 2023, a “thinking indicator” shows up in **[59 commits](https://github.com/search?q=%22thinking+indicator%22+committer-date%3A%3C2023-01-01&type=commits)** across all of public GitHub. Since then: **[roughly 20,000](https://github.com/search?q=%22thinking+indicator%22+committer-date%3A%3E2023-01-01&type=commits)**.

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8ZV1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1614d06-0576-4f13-b178-b3de57d63100_2640x1931.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!8ZV1!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe1614d06-0576-4f13-b178-b3de57d63100_2640x1931.png)

*   ✨ [~35,000 commits](https://github.com/search?q=%22sparkle+icon%22+committer-date%3A%3E2023-01-01&type=commits) touch a “sparkle icon” since 2023, 30x everything that came before. One dev swapped his chat icon for sparkles because it [“feels more AI.”](https://github.com/R4ph-t/handzon/commit/4a8403b9b2dbc9452b08ea06fa9326a56ed6f846)

*   🛡️ [~16,000](https://github.com/search?q=%22AI+badge%22+committer-date%3A%3E2023-01-01&type=commits) pin an “AI badge” somewhere on the screen.

*   🔨 Fake progress is an old trick ([5,000+ commits](https://github.com/search?q=%22fake+progress%22&type=commits) and counting), but [149 now cite the “labor illusion” by name](https://github.com/search?q=%22labor+illusion%22&type=commits) while building it.

*   🤌🏻 Some fake the wait itself: [“Add simulated delay to AI analysis for a more realistic user experience.”](https://github.com/seshankbagavath/StructuralFailureAnalysis/commit/c890292cb45e682bb5a544f598f)

*   🌀 And [~5,400](https://github.com/search?q=%22thinking+animation%22+committer-date%3A%3E2023-01-01&type=commits) add a “thinking animation”, with an open-source library offering [36 ready-made ones](https://edison7009.github.io/loading-to-thinking/).

Even the real thing is theatrical: Claude Code’s leaked source revealed 187 hardcoded [“thinking verbs”](https://x.com/wesbos/status/2038958747200962952) (words shown when it’s loading):

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Z5tU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F3fb565df-28b6-47ba-b61c-59c5bcf58064_2146x2376.png)](https://x.com/wesbos/status/2038958747200962952)

It works because the psychology is real: [a study from January](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16720) found that chatbots showing no visible “thinking” read as less warm, less engaged, and putting in minimal effort.

So if your product answers instantly or calls it “Loading...” → **users read it as the cheap one, even when it does more.**

Yes, people value things more when they see the effort behind them.

But the problem with “Thinking...” is that it’s the laziest possible way to show effort, and there are 20,000 commits on GitHub proving everyone had the same idea. So what’s the real solution?

**Show the real thing.** If your product scans 2,000 reviews, write “Scanning 2,000 reviews...” on the wait screen. No one can fake YOUR specifics.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q4P7!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe5015a6-73ab-4120-b72c-699c6b3a3636_1200x400.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Q4P7!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbe5015a6-73ab-4120-b72c-699c6b3a3636_1200x400.gif)

Much better!

**Staging the delivery is fair game too.** My [Viral Post Generator](https://www.marketingideas.com/p/viral-post-generator)‘s loading screen took exactly 10 seconds (actual loading time: 0.5 seconds). The results were real, people just got them slower, and my A/B tests showed they shared more the longer they waited.

[![Image 7](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Pk2a!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f27b309-4e4e-4626-a79b-78932adbf405_2236x1166.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Pk2a!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f27b309-4e4e-4626-a79b-78932adbf405_2236x1166.png)

I wrote a [full playbook on this exact psychology](https://www.marketingideas.com/p/how-to-make-people-pay-more-with), fake progress bars included.

Just make sure something’s actually working under the hood.

Have a great week ✌️

Tom

Title: Thumb-stopping mail

URL Source: https://www.lob.com/ebooks/thumb-stopping-mail

Published Time: Thu, 23 Jul 2026 22:42:01 GMT

Markdown Content:
Ebook

30+ creative techniques for earning 

attention in the mailbox

Contents

Introduction

About three seconds – that’s all the time your mail piece gets to earn a second glance.

The biggest challenge in direct mail isn’t getting to the mailbox on time, it’s getting noticed once it’s there. After months of careful planning, orchestration, and delivery, your campaign’s performance comes down to a single moment. How are you going to make it count?

## Standing out in the stack

People aren’t tired of communication. They’re tired of irrelevant communication.

Each day, consumers are bombarded by thousands of ads, messages, and notifications – all competing for the same limited attention. They don’t have the time to carefully read every message they come across. Instead, they do a quick scan before deciding whether to open, save, or toss. Only a fraction of readers ever even make it past the headline. To drive action, your direct mail must capture attention fast enough to leave an impression.

![Image 1](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5e1e5c62fa3d4447af417098/6a39c5552ddb95c0e294caab_marketing-alt.svg)

**On average, 5X as many people read the headline as read the body copy.**

Source: Who’s Mailing What

**How does your offer make a consumer’s life easier, better or less expensive?** The strongest pieces immediately signal relevance and authenticity. Once you’ve established that value – and given recipients a good reason to believe it – that’s when your direct mail can actually start performing.

## The essential elements of thumb-stopping mail

Thumb-stopping direct mail doesn’t try to communicate everything at once. Instead, it communicates with intention.

It sounds counterintuitive, but attention-maxxing your direct mail can do more harm than good. Cramming in too many offers, headlines, and CTAs buries your message and makes your mail easier to ignore. When everything competes for attention, nothing stands out.

After analyzing more than 1 billion+ mail sends, we’ve identified the essential elements that make direct mail easier to notice, understand, and act on.

Visual

Strong visuals make the difference between capturing attention or losing it. Eye-catching imagery and high-contrast colors stop readers in their tracks and spark an emotional connection, so they’re more likely to keep reading.

Headline

Signal immediate relevance with a bold headline that delivers your core message in just a few seconds, even if it’s the only thing your recipient reads.

Copy

Highly scannable body copy, direct language, and visual hierarchy reinforce the headline, expand your story, and guide the reader through your proof points.

CTA

A strong, simple call to action paired with multiple response paths, like QR codes, URLs, or a phone number, make it easier for recipients to convert while improving direct mail tracking and attribution.

![Image 2](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/5e1e5c62fa3d4447af417098/6a4c4f39bffb070ec15a0872_e2dfbacd2d907dbb817d0bd8fb98225e_Group%201597881882.avif)

## Thumb-stopping mail in action

From headlines that instantly communicate value to layouts that guide reader interaction, the following real-world examples demonstrate how strategic direct mail design reduces friction, builds trust, and encourages action. Here’s how.

### Anchor value first

Before anything else, your mail piece needs to prove its value by answering this question for readers, “What’s in it for me?”

What to try:

*   **Lead with benefits:** Lead with a concrete benefit that aligns with your audience’s primary motivation.
*   **Prioritize relative value over absolute value:**People rarely know if a number is good or bad in isolation. The strongest direct mail pieces provide context, such as sharing estimated mortgage rates compared to average rent costs in their area.
*   **Use personalized benchmarks:**Ground the message in data that feels specific to the recipient’s market, behavior, or situation.

What works

This real estate letter helps renters compare their current reality to a potential future one. By using personalized rent and mortgage estimates from their neighborhood, it shows that buying may be more within reach than they assumed. It also removes a major source of uncertainty by providing local benchmarks and clear next steps, making the path to homeownership feel more tangible and achievable.

### Reduce decision making

_Is this for me? Is it worth it? What do I do?_ Every extra question you force customers to answer increases their cognitive load and creates extra work for them.

The best pieces eliminate this friction by answering these questions right away – before recipients move on to the next thing.

What to try:

*   **Curate instead of overwhelm:**Organize products, services, or offers into relevant categories so recipients don't have to sort through endless options.
*   **Employ multi-channel CTAs:**Give readers one obvious next step and make it accessible across channels, whether that's a QR code, URL, phone number, or store visit.
*   **Include time-bound language:**Include offer codes with an expiration date so recipients understand when they need to act.

What works

This high-performing seasonal gift guide collapses the decision window by quickly communicating everything essential at a glance. Rather than asking recipients to browse an entire catalog, it organizes recommendations around common summer occasions, making it easier to find a relevant gift. Clear pricing, a limited-time offer, and multiple response options further reduce friction by helping readers quickly understand what to buy, why to buy it, and how to take action.

### Be specific

Consumers are naturally skeptical. Vague claims get ignored. Earn their trust with specificity. Numbers clarify your claims and create credibility.

What to try:

*   **Lead with specific values that matter most:**Make the core offer impossible to miss by putting details, such as the APY in this example, front and center.
*   **Answer key questions upfront:**Include details like rates, minimum balances, terms, and deadlines so consumers can quickly evaluate the offer.
*   **Make details easy to scan:**Group key offer information into a dedicated section so recipients can compare and understand the value at a glance.

What works

In this example, “Earn {{APY}}% on your savings” makes the value immediately clear. Instead of relying on vague promises about growing savings, the piece leads with a specific, measurable benefit and reinforces it with the details consumers need to evaluate the offer. By clearly presenting the rate, minimum balance, term length, and expiration date, it helps recipients make an informed decision without searching for additional information.

### Establish visual hierarchy

High contrast. Bold colors. Large typography. Negative space.

Strong hierarchy goes beyond a list of benefits. It’s about prioritizing information and creating a clear visual path for readers from the moment they interact with their mail.

What to try:

*   **Create a single entry point:**The oversized headline immediately establishes the primary message, helping recipients understand the offer before they engage with any supporting details.
*   **Match emphasis to value:**Reserve the strongest visual treatment for the information most likely to drive action, while secondary details support the decision without competing for attention.
*   **Sharpen the contrast:**Leverage dark, light, and accent colors to help specific information stand out.

What works

This sales event postcard doesn't treat every element equally. Through typography, contrast, and spacing, it directs readers' attention to the most important information first and lets supporting details reinforce the message. The result is a mail piece that can be understood in seconds, even by recipients who are only scanning.

### Balance emotion and logic

The highest-performing direct mail pieces use emotion to capture attention and logic to convert it.

What to try:

*   **Make an emotional appeal:**Open with an emotional hook and then reinforce it with quantifiable benefits.
*   **Use real outcomes:**Use tangible benefits to prove how your offer will make your reader’s life better.
*   **Deliver a timely message:**Target your audience with a reminder that creates urgency and personal relevance.
*   **Make next steps easy:** Bulleted steps and clear CTAs make it easy to take action across devices.

What works

This automotive postcard pairs a personal milestone with a practical benefit. The welcome message creates an emotional connection by recognizing a recent purchase, while the complimentary service offer gives readers a concrete reason to engage. Together, they make the communication feel both thoughtful and useful.

### Direct the flow

The direct mail format you use isn’t just aesthetic – it controls the way your brand’s entire story unfolds.

What to try:

*   **Make it a multi-sensory experience:**Experiment with different textures, printing techniques, and dimensional folds to give your mailer a premium feel.
*   **Try a modular layout:**Improve browsing with an engaging layout that invites readers to explore at their own pace.
*   **Build trust with copy:**Detailed, but easy-to-scan messaging adds legitimacy and inspires trust.

What works

This self-mailer uses its format to control when and how information is revealed. Rather than presenting everything at once, it breaks the claims process into manageable steps, helping readers build understanding as they move through the piece. The result is a complex topic that feels approachable instead of overwhelming.

### Make it easy to act

One CTA = one opportunity. Multiple CTAs can’t be missed.

The most successful campaigns don’t rely on just one CTA – they layer them strategically. Multiple CTAs make it easy for recipients to take action however they prefer.

What to try:

*   **Give people options, not decisions:**Offer a few ways to respond, like scanning, calling, or visiting a URL, but make sure they all lead to the same next step.
*   **Pick up where they left off:**If someone already got a quote, abandoned a cart, or started an application, make your CTA about finishing, not starting over.
*   **Tell them exactly what happens next:**Whether they'll review a quote, schedule an appointment, or claim an offer, remove the guesswork before they take action.

What works

This example leverages the sidebar to make its “Next steps” CTA section stand out. The QR code, campaign URL, and trackable phone number allow recipients to convert via their preferred channel.

### Reduce friction with familiarity

Recognition changes the way recipients view your mail. It becomes an invitation instead of an interruption. Starting with an existing relationship or an established brand gives your mail the head start it needs to get attention.

What to try:

*   **Use dynamic personalization:**Instead of sending generic mail, use a data-driven approach to personalize each piece. Even though this requires more setup and production effort, it pays off with higher engagement and ROI.
*   **Send trigger-based mail:** Go beyond basic details by sending timely mail that mirrors your customers’ recent behavior.
*   **Include branded elements:**Incorporate consistent logos, colors, and visuals in your piece so readers instantly associate it with your brand.
*   **Keep it warm:**Use language like “as a customer” or “based on your account” to reduce skepticism and build familiarity.

What works

This letter signals an existing relationship and hits both logic and emotion. It lowers reader resistance by positioning the communication as a valuable opportunity vs. a sales pitch.

### Create urgency

Urgent CTAs tend to get a bad rep. Phrases like “ACT NOW” and “LIMITED TIME ONLY” tend to sound forced and manufactured, driving recipients away.

Subtle urgency works differently by tying deadlines directly to your offer so they inform without adding pressure.

What to try:

*   **Tie urgency to the value, not the CTA:**The strongest deadlines are connected to something recipients could lose, like a discount, quote, rate, or bonus, not just an arbitrary end date.
*   **Make the window feel real:**Specific dates, expiration times, and offer periods feel more credible than generic phrases like "limited time only."
*   **Remind people what's at stake:**Reinforce what recipients gain by acting now, not just when they need to respond.

What works

This high-performing seasonal gift guide collapses the decision window by quickly communicating everything essential at a glance. Rather than asking recipients to browse an entire catalog, it organizes recommendations around common summer occasions, making it easier to find a relevant gift. Clear pricing, a limited-time offer, and multiple response options further reduce friction by helping readers quickly understand what to buy, why to buy it, and how to take action.

## Relevance gets results

The most effective direct mail campaigns are intentional from start to finish. They’re designed around how people process information: quickly and instinctively. Every element, from the copy to the color choices, should give your readers a reason to stop and pay attention. Because when mail feels clear, valuable, and relevant, performance follows.

kept.article_text:
Title: AI Content Is Everywhere on Social Media, Especially LinkedIn

URL Source: https://www.pangram.com/blog/ai-in-your-feed

Published Time: 2026-07-23T22:42:09.140Z

Markdown Content:
Two months ago, we launched [our Chrome extension](https://www.pangram.com/solutions/chrome-extension) to help combat the rising slop problem on social media. It lets users scan posts on social media as they scroll, flagging AI-generated content so they can [make informed decisions](https://www.pangram.com/blog/ai-sentiment-survey) about how they spend their attention.

Pangram is a research-first company, not just for our industry-leading AI detection algorithms, but for tracking the risk and prevalence of AI-generated content. Social media is one of the hardest domains to study here — much harder than, say, [news articles](https://www.pangram.com/ai-news), [research papers](https://www.pangram.com/blog/pangram-predicts-21-of-iclr-reviews-are-ai-generated), or [Amazon reviews](https://www.pangram.com/blog/ai-amazon-reviews). But it's also one of the most crucial, because it's potentially the highest-volume source of AI-generated content we face.

We believe it's important to understand this problem so that we can better combat it. That's why we included an opt-in setting in our Chrome extension, to allow users to aid our research by anonymously sharing their scan statistics with us. We've compiled the first few months of this data into the report below.

#### Key findings:

*   One in four longform posts on social media flagged as fully AI-generated
*   Of all posts we flagged as AI-generated, two-thirds came from LinkedIn
*   Nearly half of X/Twitter articles contained AI writing

## AI-generated content is hitting longform the hardest

AI-generated content appeared across all social media platforms in our data set. The average AI rate across all scanned items was 13.8%, but specific rates varied by platform and item length. On four out of five platforms, **longer content was more likely to be AI-generated than shortform content**. Across all platforms, one in four longform items (25.72% of items over 250 words) were fully AI-generated.

![Image 1](https://www.pangram.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2F6vunltag%2Fproduction%2F7b75f2c3b79d08f87fe4ca67de8a8fa7433e0383-2400x1260.png&w=3840&q=75)

Substack was an exception; there, the rate of fully AI-generated content remained fairly flat, and longer, more substantial posts were actually slightly less likely to be AI-generated compared to shorter ones.

LinkedIn was the most AI-saturated platform, where **more than 40% of longform posts** flagged as fully AI-generated. However, if we included mixed AI and human content, X/Twitter was the worst off: almost half of X articles were either fully AI-generated (23.9%) or [AI-assisted](https://www.pangram.com/blog/introducing-ai-assistance-detection)/mixed (22.9%), with **only 53.2% of X articles flagging as fully human-authored**.

![Image 2](https://www.pangram.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2F6vunltag%2Fproduction%2Fa46788d43a127da59b1596c750b1ce544c0122d0-1988x1040.png&w=3840&q=75)

Our data shows that AI-generated content is a problem across all platforms, and it is hitting longform content especially hard. Even Substack, which was the longform platform with the lowest combined AI rate, still saw more than a fifth of its posts (21.9%) flag as AI-generated or AI-assisted. This is consistent with the rise of AI-generated content we're seeing in writing elsewhere, such as in [newspaper opinion pieces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18774).

## AI slop is flooding LinkedIn

LinkedIn had the highest AI share of any platform across the board. LinkedIn posts made up a third of scanned items, yet it accounted for **nearly two-thirds (62%) of all AI content we flagged**. Contrary to what one might expect, people are overwhelmingly willing to use AI to speak on their behalf in professional settings that are associated with their real identity, and less likely to use it on casual and anonymous platforms.

![Image 3](https://www.pangram.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2F6vunltag%2Fproduction%2F59a04d46d70bd5d0c94ec79ab3fdc1f94d105c43-1880x1160.png&w=3840&q=75)

LinkedIn also encourages AI use on its platform in several ways, including a built-in "Write with AI" button (now rebranded "Enhance post," but still offering AI writing assistance). People are noticing LinkedIn's growing reputation for slop – perhaps to combat it, an executive at LinkedIn recently [announced](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/laura-lorenzetti_keeping-conversations-real-on-linkedin-activity-7462864768668848128-iitt) that the platform would be detecting and downranking AI-generated posts using an in-house algorithm; ironically, the announcement was itself AI-generated. Whether or not the company is attempting to modulate AI in their feed, our users are still seeing a lot of AI writing on LinkedIn.

In our data, Reddit had the highest scan volume of any platform, making up 36.7% of items that we scanned. Yet at just 4.4%, Reddit had one of the lowest combined AI shares of any platform. This is due to a **composition effect**: replies on Reddit were overwhelmingly human-authored (98.1%) and replies altogether made up 72% of Reddit items that we scanned. Top-level posts on Reddit were much more likely to be AI-written, at 11.6% of posts, in line with X/Twitter's 10.0% AI-saturation. The same pattern held on LinkedIn, albeit to a lesser extent: a top-level LinkedIn post was 1.35x more likely to be AI-generated than a comment.

![Image 4](https://www.pangram.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.sanity.io%2Fimages%2F6vunltag%2Fproduction%2F5c4ada1c32034c5f1157d45eb68f6f07b5e6a9d4-1988x700.png&w=3840&q=75)

Although LinkedIn replies were less likely to be AI-generated than posts, the effect reverses when controlling for length: LinkedIn comments were actually slightly more likely to be AI compared to top-level posts. For Reddit, the difference in AI rate was independent of post format – when controlling for length, top-level Reddit posts still had a **5.25x greater chance** of being AI-generated.

Reddit's AI-free replies point to a blind spot of many anti-botting strategies. While [Reddit's spam policy](https://techcrunch.com/2026/03/25/reddit-bots-new-human-verification-requirements/) effectively eliminates accounts that use AI to automatically generate spam replies, this approach only catches the [lowest-effort spam content](https://www.pangram.com/blog/quora-case-study) on the platform. Top-level Reddit posts only make up a quarter of all Reddit items, but they have far more audience impact, and their lower volume allows AI-authored posts to slip past volume-based moderation like rate-limiting.

## Method and data collection

Collectively, since the Chrome Extension's launch on April 24th 2026, users who opted into sharing their data for research helped us create a dataset of **1,002,627 posts** across several of the largest social media platforms on the internet: LinkedIn, Medium, Substack, X/Twitter, and Reddit. Each post in our dataset is counted only once, and we only scan items that are [longer than 50 words](https://www.pangram.com/blog/why-does-pangram-have-a-minimum-word-count). Every post was analyzed with [Pangram 3.3](https://www.pangram.com/research/model-card/pangram-3-3), our latest AI detection model, which achieves a 0.01% [false positive rate](https://www.pangram.com/blog/all-about-false-positives-in-ai-detectors). This dataset allows us a direct window into what AI-generated content people are seeing on their feeds at this point in time.

## Conclusion

**AI writing is now a problem everywhere on social media.** This is concerning, but it's in line with what we're seeing elsewhere online: [researchers estimated](https://ai-on-the-internet.github.io/) that 35% of newly published websites on the open internet were AI-generated or AI-assisted. An internet that is completely flooded with undisclosed AI content is bleak, but we don't believe it's inevitable. We hope that by providing transparency to AI-generated content online, we can give internet users back some control of how they spend their attention.

kept.heading: OPENAI APPEARS TO BE MISSING ITS SALES GOALS BY A VAST MARGIN (2 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: OpenAI's $100 billion ad-revenue target for 2030 requires three things to happen at once. Advertisers moving decades of search and social budgets into chatbots, OpenAI out-competing Google and Meta for that spend, and the entire AI ad market growing roughly 100 times from where it sits today. The category's entire addressable market currently tops out around $5.4B, and OpenAI itself is on pace to miss its own ad revenue forecast by about 90% this year.

# OpenAI Appears to Be Missing Its Sales Goals by a Vast Margin

It's a bloodbath.

![Image 4: Joe Wilkins Avatar](https://futurism.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/avatar_user_162598_1741024628.jpg?quality=85&w=102&h=102&crop=1)

By[Joe Wilkins](https://futurism.com/authors/jwilkins)

Published  Jul 20, 2026 2:30 PM EDT

[Add Futurism (opens in a new tab)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=futurism.com)More information Adding us as a Preferred Source in Google by using this link indicates that you would like to see more of our content in Google News results.

![Image 5: A photo illustration featuring OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.](https://futurism.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/openai-ad-revenue-ai-advertising-financial-projection.jpg?quality=85&w=1152)
