Even as the AI bubble becomes a mainstream [talking point](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/ai-bubble-fears-tsmc-nvidia-earnings) on Wall Street, tech companies continue to peddle the fantasy that AI is poised to become an almost magical money-maker. Case in point, OpenAI wants you to believe that by 2030, it’ll be raking in $100 billion a year just from ads alone — even though it’s currently struggling to reach just $1 billion.

That massive gulf was observed in a [new analysis](https://www.emarketer.com/content/chatgpt-ad-revenues-may-fall-90--short-of-openai-s-2030-target) from marketing consulting firm Emarketer, first [flagged by _AdWeek_](https://www.adweek.com/media/openais-ad-business-is-on-pace-to-miss-its-own-forecast-by-90-analyst-says/), which found OpenAI is on pace to undershoot its own five-year ad revenue projections by a whopping 90 percent. In fact, Emarketer’s take is even more devastating than that: it estimates the entire addressable market for chatbot advertising — the maximum amount of money up for grabs overall — at $5.4 billion.

That figure isn’t just bad news for OpenAI, but for every giant tech company, all of which are jockeying for a piece of the [AI ad pie](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/openai-perplexity-admits-ai-adverts-mistake). In 2026, Emarketer projects that the combination of OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, and Amazon will bring in under $1 billion in ad revenue. For context, OpenAI had projected that its AI ad revenue alone would hit $2.5 billion by the end of this year.

It all adds up to a difficult question for investors. If the top AI companies — which have burned over [$1.6 trillion](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/2/19/visualising-ai-spending-how-does-it-compare-with-historys-mega-projects) building AI so far — can’t even hit OpenAI’s meager projection for 2026, what hope do they have of hitting their projections four years from now?

To hit that number, _AdWeek_ observes, OpenAI needs three miracles to happen all at once. First, advertisers have to abandon decades worth of infrastructure built around search engines and social media and put all their advertising budgets into chatbots. Once that happens, OpenAI has to out-muscle previous ad-sales giants like Google and Meta, while the entire AI-ad market balloons from just a six-figure stream in 2026 to a raging, 12-figure river by 2030.

Basically, OpenAI will have to make a lot of history to justify these numbers. And whether it can do so is no small matter: according to OpenAI’s own forecasts, advertising is supposed to make up [36 percent](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/openai-forecasts-advertising-hit-102-billion-2030) of the company’s total revenue by 2030. If the AI lab can’t make the math work, the company’s five-year financial story falls apart, and with it, a major bullet point justifying one of the [largest financial bubbles](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/problem-ai-industry-collapse-efficiency) the world has ever seen.

kept.heading: COPYWRITING BREAKDOWN: HOW TO SELL SOMETHING ORDINARY (4 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Strong marketing often comes from better research instead of better copy. Claude Hopkins won customers in a crowded category by asking hundreds of consumers what they wanted, measuring how Palmolive performed against those needs, and turning the results into specific proof points. The ad replaced vague claims with numbers such as 250 times more lather, 15% water absorption in one minute, and lather that lasted 10 minutes. Research, measurable evidence, and clear messaging can make an ordinary product stand out even when competitors offer similar features.

Title: Copywriting Friday: How to sell something ordinary

URL Source: https://conversion-rate-experts.com/how-to-sell-something-ordinary-copywriting-friday/

Published Time: 2026-07-16

Markdown Content:
[Copywriting Friday](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/articles/#copywriting-friday) highlights the tools and techniques of persuasive content. Some of the examples may seem dated, but the principles are timeless (and critical for conversion rate optimization). Enjoy.

Whatever you sell, there’s a good chance others sell something similar. Strip away the branding from most categories, and many offerings do roughly the same job, roughly as well. So how do you win?

![Image 1: Close-up of the headline from a vintage Palmolive Shaving Cream advertisement.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-shaving-cream-ad-headline.jpg)

The ad we’re looking at today is a hundred-year-old answer to that question. It’s for Palmolive Shaving Cream, written by Claude Hopkins… perhaps the original conversion rate optimizer. Hopkins was blunt about the problem he faced:

> Practically all the users of shaving cream were wedded to certain brands. Perhaps most of them had used these brands for years, and they liked them. **Our problem was to win users from one brand to another.**
> 
> 
> **One can hardly claim in a shaving soap exceptional effects. That is not logical.**

Most of Hopkins’s contemporaries would have reached for louder adjectives to try [switching customers to their brand](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/switching-sales/), but he went in a different direction. Instead of trying to out-write his rivals, **he out-researched them**.

And the approach he used is a core part of our methodology, over a century later.

### 1. He asked the market what it wanted

![Image 2: Illustration of Claude Hopkins’s research men interviewing hundreds of men about shaving.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/claude-hopkins-research-men.jpg)

Before a word of copy was written, Hopkins went looking for the truth. Here’s how he described what happened in his book, _My Life In Advertising_:

> I sent out some research men to interview men by the hundreds. I asked them what they most desired in a shaving cream.

Notice what this is: voice-of-customer research, run as fieldwork, in the 1920s. Three desires came back clearly. The market wanted _abundant lather_, _quick action_ on a tough beard, and _lather that lasted_ long enough to finish the whole shave.

**That list became an input for everything that followed.** If you are trying to persuade people to buy something, _knowing what they want (in their own words)_ is extraordinarily valuable.

**How could you use this?** Our [five golden questions](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/questions/) exist to pull exactly that out of your customers. The first move in Hopkins’s method is the one that many marketers skip. If research seems like a lot of effort, keep in mind that almost all of the [Win Reports](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/articles/#win-report) we’ve published have their roots in deep research.

### 2. He measured what mattered

![Image 3: A chemist testing shaving cream in a laboratory, representing V. C. Cassidy’s work for Palmolive.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-chemist-lab-testing.jpg)

You might think that the three desires discovered above were all the gold dust Hopkins needed to create a great ad, but he had something else in mind. He took the customers’ wishlist to V. C. Cassidy, Palmolive’s chief chemist, and told him:

> These are the factors men want. They may get them in other shaving creams, but nobody yet has told them. Give me actual data on these results as applied to Palmolive Shaving Cream.

Note that Hopkins wasn’t asking the chemist to _invent_ advantages, but to _measure_ the things men already said they wanted. The figures came back one by one:

*   Men wanted abundant lather. Cassidy proved Palmolive multiplied itself in lather **250 times**.
*   Men wanted quick action. Tests showed the beard absorbed **15% of water within one minute**, enough to make the hair wax-like for cutting.
*   Men wanted lather that lasted. The chemist proved that it retained **creamy fullness for ten minutes** on the face.

Because Palmolive was the first soap company to understand what mattered to its market, it was also the first to publish hard numbers. And, as we know, [hard figures often persuade readers where adjectives bounce off](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/how-to-persuade-skeptical-people-copywriting-friday/).

**How could you use this?** Which of your general claims could you replace with a measured figure? We understand that regular readers will have seen this advice before, but we repeat it because it matters. It worked 100 years ago; it still works now.

Consider the top of our [CRO agency page](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/cro-agency/) (highlighting added):

![Image 4: Screenshot of the top of the Conversion Rate Experts CRO agency page, with measured results highlighted.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/cro-agency-page-measured-figures.jpg)

### 3. He said it out loud… first

![Image 5: A tube of vintage Palmolive Shaving Cream.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-shaving-cream-tube-1920s.jpg)

Once Hopkins had asked and measured, he could say things that no rival had bothered to say despite having similar products. Here’s a full version of the ad that Hopkins created:

![Image 6: Full page of the vintage Palmolive Shaving Cream advertisement written by Claude Hopkins.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-shaving-cream-ad-full.jpg)

Don’t be surprised to see that Hopkins highlights key aspects of the product in the left-hand column, but he doesn’t leave it there. He starts the main copy by _showing his work_:

![Image 7: Close-up of the Palmolive ad copy describing the research behind the product.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-ad-showing-the-research.jpg)

If you were a man who shaved regularly, wouldn’t you be interested in a brand that had done its research… and then delivered on _what 1,000 other men said they wanted_?

They wanted abundant lather:

![Image 8: Close-up of the Palmolive ad copy about abundant lather.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-ad-abundant-lather.jpg)

They wanted quick action:

![Image 9: Close-up of the Palmolive ad copy about quick action on the beard.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-ad-quick-action.jpg)

They wanted foam that lasted:

![Image 10: Close-up of the Palmolive ad copy about lather that lasts.](https://res.cloudinary.com/conversion-rate-experts/image/upload/w_1200,dpr_auto,c_scale,f_auto,q_auto/palmolive-ad-lather-that-lasts.jpg)

As Hopkins said:

> Probably other shaving creams could meet the same specifications… But we were the first to give figures on results. And one actual figure counts for more than countless platitudes.

Taking _ownership_ of common properties wasn’t a new strategy for Hopkins. He’d proven it decades earlier by [describing the sterilization process that Schlitz beer](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/ancient-persuaders-four-types-of-stories-that-sell-without-sounding-salesy/) (and every other brewery) used… but hadn’t mentioned to drinkers. (Advertisers would later name this technique _the preemptive claim_.)

## When you know what to say, the marketing writes itself

We could talk about the many other techniques the ad uses, but that risks obscuring the takeaway.

Strip this ad back, and the product is ordinary. Palm oil, olive oil, lather, and a shave job a dozen rivals could match. Hopkins’s method was not ordinary, but neither was it outrageously complicated or out of reach for companies today, especially given the tools we all have at our disposal:

1.   Ask your market what it wants.
2.   Measure your product or service against those desires.
3.   Be first to say them out loud, consistently, and in figures if at all possible.

**A century on, that loop is still one of the most profitable ideas in marketing.** And yet a surprising number of companies still struggle to “wear out the boot leather” when it comes to research, and consequently leave money on the table. Often, a lot of money.

Knowing your market makes everything easier. Imagine Hopkins sitting down to write, his notes at his side. With his research collected, the copy would have more or less written itself.

See you next time on [Copywriting Friday](https://conversion-rate-experts.com/articles/#copywriting-friday).

kept.article_text:
Title: Swag That Works: The New Rules for Trade Show Giveaways

URL Source: https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/swag-new-rules-for-trade-show-giveaways/

Published Time: 2026-07-20T17:00:20+00:00

Markdown Content:
![Image 1: Middesk’s exclusive merch at Money20/20 offered a glimpse at the future of business. (Photo: Anna Huddleston/Event Marketer)](https://www.eventmarketer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/swag-trends-trust-club-money2020-event-marketer-1024x902.jpg)

Middesk’s exclusive merch at Money20/20 offered a glimpse at the future of business. (Photo: Anna Huddleston/Event Marketer)

When Middesk set out to build trust with [Money20/20 attendees,](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/inside-money20-20-usa-2025-how-money-did-business/) it transformed its booth into “The Trust Club” filled with custom-designed merchandise created specifically for the trade show experience. From heavyweight crewnecks to limited-edition duffles, the brand designed exclusive items to drive engagement at different levels, all leading back to the overarching message.

“Trust is timeless, so we wanted to tap into that narrative, but also our brand is modern and nimble, and we wanted the Club to reflect that,” says Kate Young, event marketing manager at Middesk. And the merch? “We wanted it to feel like the first drop from your favorite lifestyle brand, but made for the people shaping the future of business identity.”

Branded merchandise has always held a place in trade show marketing, but it’s quickly evolving from a tactical giveaway into a strategic communication channel key to every campaign aspect, from engagement to follow-up and measurement. It’s the[keepsake long game.](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/experiential-marketing-trend-of-the-week-the-keepsake-long-game/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Some 47 percent of marketers consider branded merchandise a core marketing channel, while 82 percent of recipients feel more positive about a brand after receiving promotional products, and 87 percent keep and use branded merchandise regularly, according to recent [PPAI](https://www.ppai.org/)research. “As organizations look for marketing channels that deliver both performance and sustainability, branded merchandise offers a compelling combination of audience engagement, brand recall and environmental efficiency,” says Drew Holmgreen, PPAI president and ceo.

“Branded merchandise can align with a larger brand narrative,” says Cayce Myers, Ph.D., LL.M, J.D., APR, professor of public relations and director of graduate studies, School of Communications, Virginia Tech. “When it is intentional, relevant and value-added, it can help create identity, community and meaningful audience connections.”

Just about anything can be branded, and with AI, design ideas come fast and furious. This is how we’re seeing all this playing out on the ground.

### **Start with Strategy**

“The biggest shift is that exhibitors are starting to treat branded merchandise less like a giveaway and more like part of the overall event strategy,” says Jack Kassab, vp at Ideal Promotions. “Now the stronger brands are thinking through the full experience: what gets someone to stop, what creates a conversation, what feels useful enough to keep, and what helps the sales team follow up after the show.”

As far as product choices, Kassab is seeing an increased interest in retail-forward merchandise, curated kits, and items that feel aligned with the brand rather than generic promo products.

### **Think: Multiple Tiers**

A tiered approach is becoming an industry standard. Kassab is noticing brands developing gifting strategies based on the value of the relationship, from general booth traffic to qualified customers and VIP prospects and clients.

For Middesk, Young and her team created a menu of options: small actions for small swag with steps up to a sales meeting, client quotes about trust, and super high-quality items for VIPs who committed to a case study or event speaking engagement with the brand.

According to Young: “This gave The Trust Club a real feeling of being a retail environment to ‘go shopping’ and simultaneously the opportunity for our team to guide guests through the experience and encouraging ‘leveling up’ to the next tier if they were a good fit.”

### **Make Familiar Unique**

![Image 2: Emergent3 created custom “Safety Sodas” to break the ice with attendees at NASRO 2026.](https://www.eventmarketer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/swag-nasro-emergent3-event-marketer.jpg)

Emergent3 created custom “Safety Sodas” to break the ice with attendees at NASRO 2026.

When it comes to item selection, offering a fresh take on classic items in ways that fit the strategy is a viable approach.

“I’ve learned not to underestimate practical products,” says Dave Sarro, ceo and founder of Promo Direct. “If something earns a permanent place on a desk or in a backpack, it’s doing exactly what it was meant to do. A quality notebook, a well-designed tumbler, or a reliable tote bag can outperform something far more expensive because they become part of someone’s routine.”

Sarro says it’s not about recreating the past but about familiarity. “Products that remind people of simpler routines or everyday moments seem to resonate because they feel comfortable and authentic.”

Then how about a sleep mask and comfy socks? Wiz invited cybersecurity experts to the “Wizzz Sleep Bar” where attendees could find special prizes and get the swag that helped them sleep better and wake up with a CISO coffee kit complete with Critical Roast and Wizz Blend flavors _(see featured image)_.

What’s more familiar than a can of Coke? At the recent NASRO 2026, the national school resource officer conference, public safety app Emergent3 caught attendees’ attention with red crew pit jumpsuits and broke the ice with custom Safety Sodas—Lockdown Cola for Alert, Coordination Cola for Smart Maps, Dr. Reunify for Reunification—referencing product features. More than 500 sodas were handed out, with more than 40 meetings booked.

### **Collectible Counts**

From large tech conferences to construction and equipment trade shows, exclusive collectible items get the same crazy love as at festivals and other types of activations. CrowdStrike, for example, launched its adversary action figures at RSAC 2024 and has been adding two new adversaries each year. Among the most coveted collectibles at Hitachi events are die-cast models of machines. Plushies, pins, and nail polish colors—yes, we’re looking at you, Sherwin-Williams—continue to build engagement and connection year after year.

### **Build Your Own with AI**

From hat and charm bars to heat-press stations, personalization-rooted activations continue to win, but AI is making the offerings infinite. At [Shoptalk 2026](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/trade-show-tactics-shoptalk-2026/), for example, Optimizely brought its personalization software capabilities to life with unique scents, created right there in the booth by EveryHuman algorithmic perfumery. After being qualified by a booth staffer, attendees could scan a QR code, chat with an AI bot about their favorite scents and perfume brands, and watch their personalized perfume mixed in front of their eyes.

At [AWS re:Invent,](https://www.eventmarketer.com/article/activations-aws-reinvent-2025/) sketches and doodles came to life with the help of Amazon’s services Bedrock and SageMaker as custom stickers, a hit in the tech world and beyond. All that was required was drawing with a stylus and a little imagination, and GenAI did the rest.

![Image 3: (Photo: Anna Huddleston/Event Marketer)](https://www.eventmarketer.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/aws-swag-stickers-event-marketer-1024x704.jpg)

(Photo: Anna Huddleston/Event Marketer)

### **Follow up and Measure**

Integrating giveaways in trade show activations provides new ways for personalized and effective follow-up as well as for measuring against the brand’s KPIs. For Middesk, transparent reporting was key.

“Our team was extensively trained on how to scan leads and, through pre-set questions, quickly classify each visitor at the booth by their activities and required follow-up,” Young says. “We can see and report on those activities, the most important of which were those visitors who had taken a full meeting at the booth and required follow-up.”

The company pre-booked 160 meetings with name accounts, which completed at about 85 percent as well as added meetings from foot traffic. Young says the company generated ten times the amount spent on the activation in new pipeline, and another 26 times in influenced pipeline. “The model of gamifying swag turned out to be a great bet.”

A lower-priority goal was to grow the social media following, but a steep increase in LinkedIn followers became an unexpected success.

“By offering high-quality items—in this case, pins and luggage tags—we saw a huge leap in followers from folks genuinely interested in knowing our brand and following along with our updates,” Young says. “It surprised us how well that worked as a great supplement to the marketing team goals outside of just generating pipeline. It’s become a staple at every show.”

* * *

#### Have a story idea? Want us to cover your booth? Reach out to EM’s editor-at-large[Anna Huddleston](mailto:ahuddleston@accessintel.com).

kept.article_text:
Title: 🎙️ How I AI: How the founder of Morning Brew built a Claude content machine that never runs out of ideas

URL Source: https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/how-i-ai-how-the-founder-of-morning

Published Time: 2026-07-20T15:01:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gWeJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F361d81ef-7faf-4d8e-8028-5d5e03432a9a_2329x551.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gWeJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F361d81ef-7faf-4d8e-8028-5d5e03432a9a_2329x551.png)

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1_jlukb7gm4)

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lOtp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffe4185eb-eee3-4098-9869-2a7aa21c160f_1456x104.webp)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lOtp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffe4185eb-eee3-4098-9869-2a7aa21c160f_1456x104.webp)

> **Brought to you by:**
> 
> 
> *   **[Firecrawl](https://firecrawl.dev/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=partner&utm_campaign=how_i_ai)**—Power AI agents with clean web data
> 
> *   **[Customer.io](https://www.try.customer.io/paid/how-i-ai?utm_medium=ads&utm_source=how_i_ai&utm_campaign=ads_q3_2026_how_i_ai_podcast&utm_content=newsletter_placement_2&utm_term=demand%20gen)**—Build customer engagement campaigns from a single prompt

Claire sits down with Alex Lieberman, Co-founder and Co-Managing Partner of Tenex, to dig into the AI content system he’s built inside Claude. Alex walks through how he finds ideas, gets interviewed by AI, codifies his voice, and runs drafts through a “Writer’s Council” before posting.

1.   **The blank page is the real enemy of consistent content, and an AI Oracle makes it disappear.** Alex’s Oracle scans seven days of Slack, Notion, Gmail, and meeting notes, then surfaces 15 ranked content spikes each day—half from internal sources, half from the X and LinkedIn accounts he follows. Writing is actually the easy part; knowing what to say is where most people stall.

2.   **Map your current workflow before you touch any AI tool.** Alex’s process started with drawing out every step of content creation as it already existed, then rebuilding it from scratch with no constraints. He found that most companies discover huge inefficiencies in this step that have nothing to do with AI at all. AI just forced them to look.

3.   **AI slop is mostly a people problem, not a model problem.** Alex’s framing here is blunt: the only time the Content Machine produces slop is when the person being interviewed doesn’t share interesting enough ideas during the interview. The model is shaping clay, not inventing ideas. If the clay is bad, the sculpture will be bad.

4.   **Your voice lives in a Markdown file, and that file changes everything.** Alex’s Content Machine pulls from a personal voice guide that captures his top-performing posts, hook formulas, content structures, and even specific language patterns like “self-deprecating confidence.” The system drafts against that file, which means it’s calibrated to how Alex actually writes rather than to some average of the internet.

5.   **A reinforcement loop is how your AI system gets better every time you use it.** After every piece, Alex’s Content Machine compares the original draft to the published version, extracts generalizable lessons, and asks if they should be added to a permanent lessons file. Over time, the system stops making the same mistakes. This is the kind of feedback loop most people never build.

6.   **The interview panel is the step most people skip and the one that matters most.** The system deploys six interviewer personas (Tim Ferriss, Joe Rogan, Larry King, Howard Stern, Barbara Walters, Michael Barrow) that ask follow-up questions until they’ve extracted enough specifics to write something real. Alex voice-to-texts his answers via Wispr Flow, so every sentence in the final draft traces back to something he actually said.

7.   **Your employees are your most underleveraged marketing channel, and most companies are actively suppressing them.** Alex ran a version of employee content at Storyarb called “Own the Internet,” and it drove 40% of all inbound leads that quarter. At Tenex, he launched the Creator Cup with $5,000 in prizes to make posting feel like a team sport, not a chore. His argument to skeptical CEOs: the fastest way to lose a great employee is to make it impossible for them to build a personal brand.

8.   **A bootstrapped company can out-distribute a venture-backed one if it’s willing to show the work.** Alex’s case is simple: Tenex can’t rely on _TechCrunch_ coverage or top-tier investor mentions, so the team’s content is the visibility strategy. If the Creator Cup gets him one great engineer, the $5,000 prize pool pays back many times over compared with a recruiting agency fee. For bootstrapped companies, distribution isn’t optional, but the whole game.

9.   **The Writer’s Council won’t let a draft go out below a 9 out of 10.**Six writer personas (including a character Alex calls “the AI slop allergist”) each score the draft and run a revision loop until the aggregate clears the threshold. That scoring mechanism is also what keeps Alex from having to manually police every post, so the system holds its standard even when he’s in a hurry.

If you’re enjoying these episodes, reply and let me know what you’d love to learn more about: AI workflows, hiring, growth, product strategy—anything.

Catch you next week,

Lenny

_P.S. Want every new episode delivered the moment it drops? Hit “Follow” on your favorite podcast app._

kept.heading: HOW MUCH CREATIVE DEBT ARE YOU CARRYING? (6 MINUTE READ)
kept.blurb: Creative work needs recurring time on the calendar or it will always lose to urgent tasks. "Creative debt" is the cost of repeatedly delaying creative projects until avoiding them becomes part of your identity instead of a temporary choice. Treat creative projects like recurring commitments by scheduling dedicated time, reduce project scope, and keep momentum through small, consistent actions instead of waiting for the perfect moment. You should also remove pressure to prove ROI so creative work can exist without immediate business value. The goal is to stop delaying meaningful projects before postponement blocks future creative output.

_Hi there! You’re reading the Bonfire newsletter from Kevan Lee & Shannon Deep. If you like the types of things we talk about here, you’ll enjoy our online events and in-person retreats. **Want to hang out together in 2027? [Details here](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat).**_

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dNqs!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe92756c4-9c32-4b90-a00d-0f8334cc5864_2160x2160.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!dNqs!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fe92756c4-9c32-4b90-a00d-0f8334cc5864_2160x2160.png)

Let’s talk about something really un-fun: the concept of _debt_.

The idea of any kind of debt is that you are borrowing from your future, right? You are getting something _now_, in exchange for being able to pay for it—usually in full and then some!—at a later date.

Financial debt of course works this way, but, figuratively, so do other things. We’ve got sleep debt, technical debt, and procrastination is a kind of debt that you pay for in last-minute panic.

I’d argue there’s actually “good debt” and “bad debt,” and the difference is in the interest rate, if you follow my analogy.

We _need_ good debt, because it makes things possible that would be otherwise impossible. It costs us later, but what we pay is worth the ability to have/do something now. Good debt could be anything from literally buying a house or a car you would otherwise never have enough money for all at once, to pushing through and finishing an important project and putting off sleep, or even giving up weekends for a month to learn a new skill faster.

The figurative interest on good debt is manageable, because it’s either possible to pay a little over a long time (like responsible financial debt), or it was small to begin with (1 late night = 1 groggy morning, paid back by 1 good nap), or it converts into an investment (the skills you gained by giving up your free time are worth more to you than the month of no weekends).

But _bad_ debt is debt that racks up interest faster than you could possibly ever pay down. Meaning: the value of what you’ve received will never even out to what you owe and owe and owe.

And lately, I’ve been thinking about a kind of debt whose interest rate, I believe, is always untenably high:

Creative debt.

Creative debt occurs when we keep borrowing time from the creative projects/practice/life we’re always telling ourselves we’ll get around to later, so that we can have something else now, usually time or comfort or perceived safety. We “take” from that creative future because there are things in the present that are either more urgent or simply feel like they should be more important.

Creative debt can sound like:

*   “I’ll get back to [creative project] when work settles down.”

*   “I’ll start [creative project] after this busy season.”

*   “I’ve always wanted to learn [creative project], but it’s not productive.”

*   “I should really launch that [creative project], but it’ll change how people see me.”

*   “I miss making [creative project], but I don’t have time.”

Every time we say “not now,” or “not yet,” we’re taking out another small loan against the creatively fulfilled version of ourselves we hope to become. And while we’ll never have to pay for this debt in cash, we may end up paying for it in regrets. Or a feeling of never having fully exercised a particular muscle or scratched a specific itch.

Like all debts, creative debt starts out manageable. A few months of putting it off becomes a year, and then a year becomes five. And then suddenly, we’re not just someone who hasn’t started [creative project] yet, we’re someone who _doesn’t start things._ That’s a really dangerous narrative! Our circumstances get all confused with our identities, and we start spiraling: _Maybe I’m not disciplined enough. Maybe I’m not actually a creative person. Maybe it wasn’t really that important to me._

But I don’t think that’s true! It’s more that life is astonishingly good at filling up every nook, cranny, and crack with musts and shoulds and obligations and general _stuff to do_, and the creative parts of ourselves—the ones that don’t have deadlines or salaries or performance reviews—are always going to be the easiest to postpone.

Here’s a personal example: In 2015, I started working for a branding agency for the first time and I was no longer doing writing and script consulting gigs (my creative passions!). Coincidentally, I started a podcast with my best friend around the same time. We produced that podcast weekly for almost 7 years! It was a blast, and it was a really silly, joyful creative outlet for me, so much so that I, unknowingly, was staving off the creative debt collectors.

The podcast was allowing me to make small, regular payments on my creative debt, and I didn’t even realize it. I honestly just kind of thought that I didn’t really “miss” writing and theater that much—that I must _not_ have an unslakable thirst to make things like I thought.

Then the podcast ended in 2022…and _boy, did I notice_! I was shocked at how uncomfy I felt, how bored and unsatisfied I was at work, and how much “extra” energy I suddenly had to create. (I started some long-term creative projects and haven’t stopped.)

All that to say: Your creative identity is _always_ _important, but not often urgent_. Because, as we’ve discussed at length elsewhere, what your creativity needs is[time, space](https://aroundthebonfire.substack.com/p/series-building-your-creative-practice-0e0?utm_source=kevans-newsletter-efd625.beehiiv.com&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=series-building-your-creative-practice-work), [safety](https://newsletter.aroundthebonfire.com/p/41-five-tricks-to-put-your-brain?utm_source=publication-search), and [permission](https://newsletter.aroundthebonfire.com/p/series-building-your-creative-practice-910?utm_source=publication-search) to actually unfurl! “Hurry up and be creative in this little box! GO GO GO! ” isn’t usually going to beget very fruitful conditions.

Kevan and I have talked a lot about this and how we support our creative identities while still running Bonfire. How do we both pay back any debt we’ve accrued while working in in-house roles that sapped our creativity, and how do we ensure that we’re not unthinkingly adding to our tabs again?

Since the beginning of 2026, we’ve put our money where our mouths are: Fridays are creative days. We work, but it’s not Bonfire work; it’s our personal creative projects, both of which happen to be long-form writing at the moment!

Basically, we’ve given ourselves a container with all the key ingredients:

*   **Time:**Once a week, every week, instead of just squeezing creative work into evenings or weekends—time that should be for family, friends, and restorative things!

*   **Space:** We don’t schedule meetings or deliver work to clients on Fridays. We give ourselves room from other obligations.

*   **Safety:** We discussed ahead of time what expectations are so we get all necessary work done without disappointing or overburdening each other.

*   **Permission:**We explicitly talked about structuring our business in ways that support our creative life. It’s a goal of ours, and it’s empowering to give ourselves permission to do so!

This is why the concept of a creative retreat works. It takes you out of your day-to-day and hands you the four elements above on a platter. You’re there for a dedicated amount of time, for an explicit purpose, with others in the same boat!

_Spoiler: One of them is our [new creative retreat](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat)!_

If we extend the metaphor and beat it to absolute death (sorry), then the goal isn’t “be more creative”; it’s to _stop borrowing from your future creative self._

Here are some ways to think about paying down creative debt:

**1. Stop taking out new loans.**This always comes before paying off old ones! When new conflicts with your creative projects come up, ask, “Is this something I actually want to do at the expense of my creativity?” That new framing might make it easier to say no!

**2. Make interest-only payments.**Maybe you don’t _finish_ the movie or novel. Instead, you just keep the relationship alive. Write for 10 minutes a day. Practice one song. Sketch for a commercial break. Tiny acts prevent creative debt from compounding. (See: My podcast example.)

**3. Consolidate your debt, or renegotiate the terms.**You might very well have 27 unfinished projects. Choose _one_, or “renegotiate” your ambitions to make them more immediately achievable. For example:

*   The novel becomes short stories

*   The pop-up restaurant becomes monthly dinner parties

*   The band becomes releasing singles online

Just like financial debt consolidation, fewer or less expensive obligations make progress feel possible.

**4. Evaluate what other debts you’re paying on.**Sometimes paying down creative debt means deliberately giving _slightly less_ attention to something else. What else is negotiable in your life?

**5. Create automatic payments.**This is my favorite metaphor! (Also, I told you we were beating it to death!) Nobody pays every bill manually anymore, so why try to pay your creative debt that way? What Kevan and I do on Fridays is a version of this. Automatic payments mean creating recurring containers: Saturday mornings, one retreat every year, monthly writing group, etc.

**6. Stop calculating ROI.**Creative debt grows because every creative act has to justify itself, either financially or by our other (often external or imagined) [standards of success](https://newsletter.aroundthebonfire.com/p/3-ways-to-redefine-creative-success?utm_source=publication-search): _Can I sell it? Will anyone read it? Will this become my career?_ The quickest way to reduce creative debt is to make something whose only purpose is to exist.

**7. Pay the highest-interest debt first.**Not all neglected projects weigh equally, do they? Some haunt you. Others just seem fun. Ask yourself: _Which unfinished thing do I think about most often? What will I regret most if I don’t pursue it?_ That’s the one accruing the most psychological interest.

**8. Declare bankruptcy.**(Almost done torturing this metaphor!) Some creative ambitions belong to a former version of you. You don’t have to carry them forever! The goal isn’t completing every abandoned project; it’s making room for the ones feel most vital and vibrant to you NOW.

**9. Make a lump-sum payment.**Sometimes years of accumulated creative debt can’t be addressed in 20-minute increments. This is where we have something concrete to offer: our new creative retreat, which we’re calling **[The Excuse](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat)**.

This is a dedicated 5 days in the French countryside just for (finally!) working on whatever it is that lights you up. Beautiful surroundings, your own private room, comfy communal spaces, a supportive environment, safe ways to share your work, and all your meals provided by a private chef.

Our [past retreats](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/experiences) were about reconnecting with your desires and motivations, both personally and professionally. And what we’ve got scheduled for 2027 is the next phase: take the first step to bring your creative ambitions to life.

We’ve got [3 different dates](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat#retreat-calendar)in 2027 on the calendar right now. Browse all the details [here](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat), and reach out at any time with questions!

So, what creative debt are you carrying? What’s the book, the painting practice, the podcast, the hobby, or the dream you’ve been borrowing from for years? We’d love to hear about it!

If you need help with brand strategy and storytelling, fractional brand and marketing leadership, and bringing your brand strategy to life in impactful ways, send us an email at **hello@aroundthebonfire.com** to get in touch.

We do in-person retreats…and our 2027 calendar is live! Browse [all the details here](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat), or [sign up for the mailing list](https://www.aroundthebonfire.com/creative-retreat#retreats-list) to find out when we have new ones to offer.

We’ve got a bunch of [digital events on the calendar](https://luma.com/calendar/cal-1XaDo5zKqQluaTD). We’d love to see you there.

As always, you can find us on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/aroundthebonfire/?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Ad_flagship3_search_srp_all%3ByIDXn%2BW7RO2OHyL9j5YfeQ%3D%3D), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/yaybonfire/), and [Threads](https://www.threads.net/@yaybonfire?xmt=AQGzvQXNJs4dWP9KRQvp1DsdedF9t_K3Eaa6IZGBFrpQrfs).

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PbRE!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F47cc3c1e-3943-4df3-84a1-ff523edd66cf_854x372.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PbRE!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F47cc3c1e-3943-4df3-84a1-ff523edd66cf_854x372.png)

kept.blurb: Head term queries are what fund Google's ad business, since two-word category terms draw 5x to 15x the CPC of longtail equivalents, and those same head terms are now shrinking in 7 of 9 consumer categories. Entertainment's head term volume fell 16% year over year, the sharpest decline in the dataset, in a category where AI tools already give users a credible substitute for a Google search entirely. Title: Why Your Top Keywords Are Quietly Losing Volume

URL Source: https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/ai-overviews-declining-keyword-volume/

Published Time: 2026-07-20T17:36:48+00:00

Markdown Content:
Brainlabs analysed 1.35 million keywords across nine categories of UK search. The findings are unambiguous. Head terms are in structural decline in seven of nine categories. Longtail is growing. AI Overviews are concentrating exactly where the volume is heading. For brands that depend on organic search, the window to adapt is narrowing.

![Image 1](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-15-1024x194.png)
## **The study that prompted this research — and the two questions it left unanswered**

In August 2025, Semrush published a study that made headlines across the SEO industry. Analysing 260 billion rows of clickstream data, they tracked how users’ Google behaviour changed after their first interaction with ChatGPT.

Their conclusion:[ChatGPT is not replacing Google — it’s expanding search](https://www.semrush.com/blog/google-usage-after-chatgpt-adoption/). Users who adopted ChatGPT showed no statistically significant decline in daily Google sessions. If anything, overall search activity ticked up slightly.

![Image 2](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-16.png)

That finding could be interpreted as reassuring. I’d argue it shouldn’t be. The Semrush study measured whether people still use Google. It did not measure what they’re searching for when they get there, or what Google is showing them when they do. Those are different questions — and they’re the questions that matter most to brands trying to understand their organic visibility and paid search strategy over the next two years.

Google itself has stated publicly that average query length is increasing. Users are asking longer, more conversational questions, a pattern that predates AI Overviews but has accelerated sharply since. And our clients are seeing it directly: head term traffic softening, longtail queries growing, and AI Overviews appearing in places that go well beyond the purely informational queries where most people assume they sit.

So we pulled 1.35 million keywords across nine UK categories from Ahrefs and ran the analysis ourselves. Two hypotheses drove the work.

#### **1. AI adoption is reshaping query composition inside Google — not just overall volume**

People may still use Google at the same frequency, but what they search for is changing. AI tools are training users to ask longer, more specific questions. Head terms — the short, high-volume queries that have historically driven the most value — should be declining. Longtail and potentially branded queries should be growing. The Semrush study doesn’t address this. Ours does.

**Verdict below: largely confirmed in 7 of 9 categories**

#### **2. AI Overviews are appearing on commercial queries, not just informational ones**

The conventional wisdom is that Google deploys AIOs on informational queries — how-to, what-is, research-type searches — and keeps commercial SERPs clean to protect ad revenue. Our hypothesis is that this is only partially true, and that AIOs are already appearing across a broader keyword set including mid-funnel commercial queries. If correct, the click-suppression risk is more significant than most brands have planned for.

**Verdict below: confirmed — AIO rate on longtail is 2–3× head terms across all categories**

**A note on methodology.**Our analysis measures search volume trends at keyword level using Ahrefs data — a different lens to Semrush’s session-frequency approach. The two studies are complementary, not contradictory. Semrush answers: are people still using Google? We answer: what are they searching for when they do, and what are they seeing when they get there? Both questions matter. The second one has more direct implications for organic and paid strategy.

* * *

## **AIO coverage ranges from 6.9% to 43.9% — and the gap is not random**

Google is deploying AI Overviews very differently across sectors. The variation reflects deliberate intent classification, not inconsistency in the algorithm.

![Image 3](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-17-1024x347.png)

Petcare sits at the top because the category is saturated with informational queries. “What can dogs eat”, “is chocolate toxic to cats”, “how often should I worm my rabbit” — these are questions Google is confident AI can answer well, and answer accurately. Petcare rewards an AI-first content approach.

Energy sits at the bottom for the opposite reason. Most energy queries are navigational or commercially specific. “British Gas contact number”, “cheapest electricity provider”, “OVO Energy tariffs 2026” — Google recognises the liability of generating AI answers for queries where being wrong costs someone real money, and holds back accordingly.

Consumer electronics (36.7%) and beauty (30.6%) sit in the middle-upper range, both driven by strong research and comparison behaviour.

![Image 4](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-20.png)

Travel (23.5%) and motor vehicles (23.3%) are almost identical despite having quite different demand profiles, which suggests a shared dynamic around commercial intent suppressing AIO deployment. Entertainment (12.0%) and crafting (11.7%) share a low AIO rate despite being informational categories — a finding worth interrogating, and one we return to below.

* * *

## **Longtail queries attract AI Overviews at nearly twice the rate of head terms — in every category**

Across all nine categories without exception, the volume-weighted AIO rate for longtail queries (4+ words) consistently outpaces head and mid-length terms (1–3 words). In several categories the gap is dramatic. [See below for an explanation of volume-weighted and methodology](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/p/39105ce3375780b7ae1bfc5e50b92fde?pvs=25#39f05ce337578051b8c2f4df22ded3b5).

![Image 5](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-19-1024x348.png)
Petcare shows the widest gap: 20.8% for head terms against 58.5% for longtail. Consumer electronics is close behind at 18.5% versus 51.8%. The pattern tells a consistent story — Google sees longtail queries as the territory where AI-generated answers add the most value to users, and head terms as the territory where it proceeds with more caution, more often deferring to traditional ranked results.

Motor vehicles is the one genuine exception. The gap between head and longtail AIO rates is the smallest of any category (15.1% vs 23.4%), and the longtail premium barely exists. Car buying is a high-commercial-intent journey across almost all query types, and Google treats nearly all of it as too consequential for AI-generated shortcuts.

For brands in categories like petcare and consumer electronics, longtail optimisation is no longer just a traffic play. Being cited in an AI Overview for high-intent longtail queries is now a meaningful visibility objective in its own right, distinct from and complementary to traditional ranking.

> _**“In petcare, longtail has nearly three times the AIO rate of head terms. That gap defines where AI disruption is concentrated — and where the content opportunity is sharpest.”**_

![Image 6](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-21.png)

* * *

## **Head terms are losing search volume in seven of nine categories**

The year-on-year trend for head and mid-length terms (1–3 words) tells a consistent story of structural decline, with entertainment and home improvement leading the fall and only consumer electronics showing meaningful growth.

![Image 7](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-22-1024x347.png)

![Image 8](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-23.png)

Entertainment’s -16% YoY decline is the sharpest in the dataset. It also happens to be the category where AI tools are the most credible substitute for Google. If you want to know what to watch tonight, ChatGPT, Perplexity or a streaming platform’s own recommendation engine can answer that without a SERP. The query is not migrating within Google — in many cases it is leaving the platform altogether.

Home improvement (-8.8%), energy (-7.4%) and crafting (-6.8%) are all in meaningful decline. Travel (-5.2%) is the most alarming in absolute terms: with 165 million head term searches in the dataset, a 5.2% decline represents tens of millions of lost impressions annually, and 69.6% of individual keywords are already declining.

Consumer electronics (+9.7%) and beauty (+0.5%) are the outliers. Electronics is driven by the AI device supercycle — new product launches, spec comparisons and upgrade queries are generating genuine head term volume growth. Beauty reflects the continued strength of social-media-driven discovery, with trend-led search terms pulling up category-level head queries. Neither should be assumed permanent: the consumer electronics forecast already shows signs of deceleration at -4.7% projected for the coming twelve months.

* * *

## **As head terms fall, longtail is mostly compensating — but not always**

Placing head and longtail YoY trends side by side reveals the scale of divergence. In most categories, the gap is significant. In only two categories are both longtail and head term volumes moving in a positive direction (Beauty and Consumer Electronics). And one (Motor Vehicles) where both are declining.

![Image 9](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-24-1024x347.png)
Entertainment shows the most dramatic divergence: head terms falling at -16% while longtail grows at +62.1% YoY. The scale of that longtail surge reflects a genuine structural shift in how entertainment queries are being formed. Users who once searched two-word terms like “Netflix shows” or “best films” are now asking longer, more specific questions: “what should I watch on Netflix if I liked Severance”, “best British crime drama 2026”, “feel-good films to watch on a Sunday”. Google is answering many of those with AI. The volume of such queries is growing fast.

Home improvement (+14.7% longtail, -8.8% head) and petcare (+13.2% longtail, -4.1% head) show a similar dynamic at smaller scale. The head term decline is real, but the longtail growth provides meaningful partial compensation in total volume terms, and the longtail queries carry higher AIO exposure, which changes the visibility calculus.

Motor vehicles breaks the pattern entirely. Both head and longtail are declining, suggesting the migration is away from Google altogether, towards OEM apps, dealer configurators and platform-specific automotive search tools. There is no longtail recovery to point to here. It is the most structurally challenged category in the dataset.

![Image 10](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-25-1024x146.png)

* * *

## **All nine categories — complete figures**

![Image 11](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-28-1024x362.png)
> **Methodology:**Analysis based on 1.35 million Ahrefs keyword exports across nine UK categories, captured May 2026. Historical search volume data covers May 2024 to April 2026 (24 months). Forecast data covers May 2026 to May 2027. AIO presence identified via SERP Features column. Volume-weighted AIO rates calculated by weighting each keyword’s AIO flag against its monthly search volume. Head/mid terms defined as 1–3 words. Longtail defined as 4+ words. YoY trend calculated by comparing average monthly search volume, Year 1 (May 2024–April 2025) vs Year 2 (May 2025–April 2026).

* * *

## **Ranking is not enough. Three objectives now exist where one used to.**

![Image 12](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-26.png)

The longtail shift is real, and it demands a different strategic response than simply producing more content. The problem is that longtail is now the highest-exposure zone for AI Overviews. Across the nine categories, volume-weighted longtail AIO rates range from 23.4% to 58.5%. Being ranked position one for a longtail query no longer guarantees meaningful traffic if an AIO sits above you and resolves the intent without a click.

Optimising for AIO citation is now a parallel objective to ranking. That requires authoritative, well-structured content with clear, verifiable claims — not the broad, hedged, “comprehensive guide to X” articles that tend to perform well in traditional organic rankings. Google cites sources it trusts. Trust here means specificity, demonstrable expertise, and factual precision on the exact question being asked. Most brands’ content libraries are not built for this.

A third objective also exists in high-AIO categories: zero-click brand presence. When an AIO cites your brand as a source, you gain credibility and awareness even if the user never clicks through to your site. Measuring that exposure requires different frameworks to traditional organic traffic reporting. Most analytics setups are not capturing it.

The volume composition of most categories means head term decline hits harder than the percentages suggest. Head and mid-length terms still account for 65–85% of total search volume across most sectors. Travel’s 165 million head term searches versus 28 million longtail is the extreme example of a pattern that appears throughout the data. Losing 5–17% of head term volume is a larger absolute hit than gaining 15–62% on a smaller longtail base, in every category except entertainment.

> _**“Most brands are optimising for a SERP that is gradually becoming less relevant to the queries where they most need to be visible. The longtail AIO rate is not a future problem — it is a present one.”**_

The two growing categories warrant a different approach. Consumer electronics and beauty are both currently in positive volume territory across head and longtail tiers. For brands in those sectors, more aggressive content investment is justified right now — the demand is there in a way it is not in entertainment, crafting or energy. That window may not last. The consumer electronics forecast already shows deceleration, and beauty’s head term growth is modest enough that one poor product cycle or trend reversal could turn it negative.

* * *

Google’s advertising business is disproportionately dependent on high-volume head term auctions. A travel brand, energy supplier or entertainment platform bidding on a two-word category term pays five to fifteen times the CPC of a four-word longtail query. Head terms drive auction depth. Auction depth drives CPC inflation. CPC inflation drives Google’s revenue per search. The mathematics of this dependency are not complicated.

If head term volume is falling 5–16% annually in several major categories, the auction economics deteriorate. There are fewer impressions to bid on. Fewer advertisers competing for the same impression pushes CPCs down, even if individual advertiser budgets hold flat. The categories where this risk is sharpest are entertainment (-16% YoY), energy (-7.4% with a further -8.9% forecast), home improvement (-8.8%) and crafting (-6.8%). Travel is the most concerning in absolute terms — the volume base is the largest in this dataset, and 69.6% of individual keywords are already declining.

> _**“Google is deploying AI Overviews heavily on longtail queries and being conservative on commercially sensitive head terms. That pattern looks like deliberate revenue protection, not algorithmic coincidence.”**_

Longtail growth partially compensates. More longtail queries means more ad impressions, and those impressions often carry genuine commercial intent. But the revenue per click is materially lower, inventory is more fragmented, and match type complexity increases. Google would need substantially more longtail volume growth to offset head term revenue decline at scale. The current data does not show that happening at the required rate, outside consumer electronics and entertainment.

The more serious long-term risk for Google is not that AI Overviews directly cannibalise ad revenue on existing searches — it is that users who previously arrived at Google for informational head term queries are now going to ChatGPT, Gemini or other AI tools, and never reaching a SERP at all. That missing query does not migrate within Google. It simply does not appear in the data. Entertainment and crafting are strong candidates for this kind of silent attrition: knowledge and inspiration categories where conversational AI is a genuinely credible substitute for a Google search.

For paid search advertisers, the short-term implication is that head term CPCs in declining-volume categories may rise before they fall, as constrained supply meets similar demand pressure. After that, the dynamics depend on whether advertisers follow the volume migration into longtail or maintain head term budget allocations for brand visibility reasons. Most large advertisers will do both, which slows the adjustment. But the adjustment is happening, and the categories above suggest its scale.

![Image 13](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/image-27-1024x145.png)

* * *

## **How the data was gathered and analysed**

**Data source.**All keyword data was exported from[Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/), one of the leading SEO data platforms. Ahrefs crawls the web continuously and collects live SERP data at scale, including which SERP features appear for any given keyword at any given time. AI Overview presence is tracked as a SERP feature within Ahrefs’ keyword data.

**Dataset size and scope.**The analysis covers 1.35 million keywords across nine UK consumer categories: petcare, motor vehicle, entertainment, consumer electronics, travel, beauty, crafting, energy, and home improvement. Each category dataset contains up to 150,000 keywords. All keywords are UK (gb) search queries captured in May 2026.

**AIO identification.**A keyword was classified as having an AI Overview if “AI Overview” appeared in the SERP Features column of the Ahrefs export. Volume-weighted AIO rates were calculated by weighting each keyword’s AIO flag against its monthly search volume, giving a more representative picture than a simple count of keywords.

**A note on volume-weighting and why we use it:** If we take a category e.g. Petcare, we have 150,000 keywords per category, but “dog food” gets 500,000 searches a month and “labrador puppy grain-free wet food pouches” gets 50. If we just counted how many keywords have an AIO, those two keywords would count equally — but “dog food” is 10,000× more relevant to what users actually experience.

So instead, we ask: of all the search volume in this category, what proportion of it is exposed to an AI Overview? That’s the volume-weighted rate.

So for head terms in Petcare, it looks like this:

1.   Sum up the search volume for every head keyword where AIO = yes → call that A
2.   Sum up the search volume for every head keyword → call that B
3.   Head AIO % = A ÷ B = 20.8%

If we’d just done count-based (keywords with AIO ÷ total keywords), we’d get a different number — and it would be skewed by thousands of niche long-tail head terms with tiny volumes.

The one place we _did_ use count-based is the **Overall AIO %** column — because there we wanted to answer a slightly different question: “what share of keywords in this space even have an AIO at all?” That’s a content coverage question, not a traffic exposure question, so count-based is actually the right tool for it.

**Search volume trends.**Ahrefs provides a monthly search volume time series for each keyword. The historical series covers May 2024 to April 2026 (24 data points). The forecast series covers May 2026 to May 2027 (13 data points), generated using Ahrefs’ own forecasting model. Year-on-year trends were calculated by comparing the average monthly volume across Year 1 (May 2024–April 2025) against Year 2 (May 2025–April 2026). Keywords with incomplete series were excluded from trend calculations.

**Keyword classification.**Keywords were classified by word count: 1–3 words as head/mid terms, 4 or more words as longtail. This is a standard industry classification and aligns with how query intent typically shifts as length increases. All volume-weighted figures use the Ahrefs-reported monthly search volume as the weighting factor.

**Limitations.**AIO presence is a point-in-time snapshot — Google’s AI Overview deployment changes frequently. Ahrefs’ SERP crawls do not capture every query at every moment, so rates reflect a strong sample rather than a census. Forecast data is modelled and should be treated as directional rather than definitive.

### **Want to know where _your category stands?_**

Brainlabs runs this analysis against specific client keyword sets as part of our SEO and Paid Search strategy work. If your sector is not in this dataset, or you want a deeper cut of your own data, talk to the SEO team.

[Talk to our SEO team](https://www.brainlabsdigital.com/contact/)
